The findings that should prompt referral to a genetic counsellor are specific: a known inherited condition; two or more miscarriages; a stillbirth or neonatal death; a child or close relative with a birth defect, intellectual disability or developmental delay; early-onset cancer clusters; consanguinity, meaning parents who are related, which raises the chance both carry the same rare recessive variant; or ancestry from a population with a recognised founder condition. Advanced paternal age, generally above 40 to 45, modestly raises the rate of new dominant mutations, a different mechanism from the maternal-age chromosomal risk.

Screening has real limits that should be stated plainly. A negative result reduces risk but never eliminates it, because no panel covers every variant of every gene. Results can be ambiguous, reported as variants of uncertain significance, which are genuinely difficult to act on. And results carry implications for siblings and existing children, which some people would rather not know. Counselling before testing, not only after, is what makes the process useful rather than merely alarming.

sections.heading: Age, Fertility Decline and Realistic Expectations
sections.body:
Female fertility declines with age through a mechanism that is well understood and cannot presently be reversed. Unlike sperm, which are produced continuously, oocytes are made once. A female fetus has around six to seven million oocytes at twenty weeks of gestation, about one to two million at birth, and roughly 300,000 to 400,000 at puberty. From then, follicles are lost continuously through atresia, with only about 400 ever ovulated across a reproductive lifetime. The decline in quantity accelerates after about age 37. Quality declines in parallel and matters more: the chance that an oocyte carries a chromosomal abnormality, most often from errors in meiotic segregation of chromosomes held in arrest for decades, rises steeply with age.

The numbers are worth stating concretely, while remembering that they are population averages and say nothing definite about an individual. Monthly conception probability is roughly 20 to 25 per cent in the early twenties, around 15 per cent at 35, and under 5 per cent at 40. The risk of trisomy 21 at birth is approximately one in 1,500 at age 20, one in 900 at 30, one in 350 at 35, one in 100 at 40, and about one in 30 at 45. Miscarriage rates follow the same curve, from roughly 10 to 12 per cent in the twenties to 25 per cent at 40 and above 50 per cent past 45, driven mainly by aneuploidy. Rates of gestational diabetes, hypertensive disorders, placenta praevia, caesarean delivery and stillbirth all rise with maternal age, though the absolute risks in a healthy 38-year-old remain modest.

Ovarian reserve testing, using anti-Müllerian hormone and antral follicle count on ultrasound, measures how many follicles remain. It predicts response to fertility drugs reasonably well, which is its legitimate clinical use. It is a poor predictor of natural fertility, and a low result in someone conceiving naturally should not be read as a verdict. This distinction is frequently blurred in commercial testing marketing.

Male fertility declines too, more gradually. Semen volume, motility and normal morphology decline from around age 40, DNA fragmentation rises, and the rate of new mutations in sperm increases with each paternal year, contributing to a small absolute rise in achondroplasia, Apert syndrome and possibly autism and schizophrenia. Time to conception lengthens measurably when the male partner is over 45.

The practical response is not panic but arithmetic. If you want two or three children and are 36, the timeline is different from wanting one at 30. Oocyte cryopreservation is a genuine option, most effective when performed before 35, with success falling sharply after 38; it should be presented honestly, since per-oocyte live birth rates mean a meaningful number of stored eggs is required.

sections.heading: The Male Partner: Sperm Health and Shared Responsibility
sections.body:
Roughly 40 to 50 per cent of infertility involves a male factor, either alone or alongside a female factor, yet preconception advice is still routinely addressed only to the person who will carry the pregnancy. This is both unfair and clinically wrong. Sperm production, spermatogenesis, takes about 74 days from stem cell to mature spermatozoon, with a further two weeks or so of maturation in the epididymis. That means changes made today alter the sperm being ejaculated in roughly three months, which is precisely why the three-month preconception window applies to both partners.

The testes sit outside the body because spermatogenesis requires a temperature about two to four degrees Celsius below core temperature. Anything that defeats that arrangement reduces sperm production: frequent hot baths and saunas, prolonged laptop use directly on the lap, extended driving without breaks, and, more importantly than most realise, obesity, which insulates the scrotum and also converts testosterone to oestrogen in adipose tissue. Varicocele, a dilated network of scrotal veins present in around 15 per cent of men and up to 40 per cent of those with infertility, raises scrotal temperature and is potentially correctable surgically.

Smoking reduces sperm count, motility and normal morphology and increases DNA fragmentation. Heavy alcohol use suppresses testosterone and impairs sperm production. Anabolic steroids are a common and under-disclosed cause of profound suppression, since exogenous testosterone shuts down the pituitary signals that drive spermatogenesis; recovery after stopping takes many months and is occasionally incomplete. Some prescription medicines matter too, including sulfasalazine, certain calcium channel blockers, spironolactone, chemotherapy agents and finasteride. Cannabis affects motility. Heat, toxins, radiation and pesticide exposure at work are all documented contributors.

Diet and body composition matter in the expected direction. Antioxidant-rich diets, adequate zinc, selenium and folate, regular moderate exercise, and normalising body weight all show modest improvements in semen parameters. The evidence for antioxidant supplements specifically is mixed and often based on small trials; a reasonable position is that a good diet is well supported while expensive supplement stacks are not.

Semen analysis is the diagnostic test, and it should be requested early rather than after a year of investigating the female partner alone. It is cheap, non-invasive and informative. Current World Health Organization reference values, revised in 2021, place the fifth-centile thresholds at approximately 1.4 millilitres volume, 16 million sperm per millilitre, 39 million total sperm, 42 per cent total motility, 30 per cent progressive motility and 4 per cent normal forms. These are reference limits from men whose partners conceived within a year, not sharp cut-offs between fertile and infertile; a result slightly below one threshold is not a diagnosis. Because counts vary considerably, an abnormal result should be repeated after about three months before conclusions are drawn.

sections.heading: Mental Health, Stress, Sleep and Practical Support
sections.body:
Mental health is not a soft addendum to pregnancy planning. Perinatal mental illness affects roughly one in five women, suicide is a leading cause of maternal death in the year after birth in several high-income countries, and untreated maternal depression is itself associated with preterm birth, low birth weight and impaired mother-infant interaction. The preconception period is when medication decisions should be made calmly rather than during a first-trimester crisis.

The central dilemma is real and should not be resolved by reflex. Untreated illness carries risk; medication carries risk; and the relevant comparison is between them, not between medication and an imaginary risk-free state. Most selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors have been extensively studied, with sertraline often preferred; paroxetine has been associated with a small absolute increase in cardiac defects in some studies, an association that has weakened as confounding by indication has been better controlled. Late-pregnancy exposure can produce a transient neonatal adaptation syndrome, usually mild and self-limiting. Lithium requires specialist supervision because of a rare association with Ebstein's anomaly and because blood levels shift with pregnancy physiology. Sodium valproate is contraindicated when used as a mood stabiliser in anyone who might conceive. Abruptly stopping an effective antidepressant on discovering a pregnancy carries a high relapse rate and is generally the worst available option.

Certain histories predict risk strongly enough to justify a plan made in advance. A previous episode of postpartum psychosis carries a recurrence risk of roughly 50 per cent, which makes prophylactic treatment and an agreed monitoring plan a reasonable proposal. Bipolar disorder, previous severe depression, a history of trauma or previous traumatic birth, and eating disorders all warrant a named clinician and a written plan before conception rather than a referral made at 30 weeks.

Ordinary stress is a different question and is frequently over-blamed. There is no good evidence that everyday stress prevents conception, and telling someone struggling to conceive to relax is both unkind and unsupported. Severe, chronic stress does affect the hypothalamic-pituitary axis and can disrupt ovulation, and there is a plausible association between very high stress and preterm birth, but the everyday version does not deserve the guilt attached to it.

Sleep is more actionable than it appears. Short sleep and untreated obstructive sleep apnoea are associated with gestational diabetes and hypertensive disorders, and both are more treatable before pregnancy than during it. Shift work, particularly rotating nights, is associated in cohort data with menstrual irregularity and modestly increased miscarriage risk.

Practical support belongs in the same conversation. Establish who will help in the first six weeks after birth, what parental leave both partners are entitled to and how it will be split, how the household finances absorb reduced income, and whether housing is adequate. Screening for domestic abuse belongs here too, because pregnancy is a recognised period of escalation rather than protection.

sections.heading: The Positive Test and the First Twelve Weeks
sections.body:
Home pregnancy tests detect the beta subunit of human chorionic gonadotropin in urine. Sensitive tests detect concentrations around 20 to 25 international units per litre, which is typically reached about 12 to 14 days after ovulation, or around the day of a missed period. Testing earlier produces false negatives because implantation may not yet have occurred; the advice to retest in three days after a negative result with a missed period is sound. False positives are uncommon but occur after a recent miscarriage, with certain fertility drugs containing hCG, and rarely with some tumours.

Dating uses the first day of the last menstrual period, which places the notional start of pregnancy about two weeks before conception. Naegele's rule gives an estimated due date by adding one year and seven days to that date and subtracting three months. Only about 4 per cent of babies arrive on that exact day, and an ultrasound between 8 and 13 weeks dates the pregnancy more accurately than any calendar calculation, particularly in irregular cycles.

Bleeding in early pregnancy is common, occurring in around a quarter of pregnancies, and roughly half of those continue normally. It nonetheless always warrants assessment, because the alternative diagnoses matter. Ectopic pregnancy, where implantation occurs outside the uterine cavity, most often in a fallopian tube, occurs in about 1 to 2 per cent of pregnancies and is a genuine surgical emergency; the classic presentation is one-sided lower abdominal pain with bleeding around six to eight weeks, and shoulder-tip pain or faintness suggests intra-abdominal bleeding requiring immediate care.
steps: Confirm with a home urine test from the first day of a missed period; if negative but the period does not arrive, repeat in three days using first-morning urine, which is most concentrated.

Start or continue 400 micrograms of folic acid daily, or the higher 5 milligram dose if you fall into a high-risk group, plus 10 micrograms of vitamin D, and continue folic acid to the end of week twelve.
Stop alcohol entirely, stop smoking and vaping, cap caffeine at 200 milligrams daily, and stop any non-essential supplement containing retinol.

Contact a midwife or doctor within the first week to book antenatal care; in many systems the first booking appointment is targeted at 8 to 10 weeks and access to screening depends on booking promptly.
List every medicine you take and ask specifically whether each should be continued, substituted or stopped, and do not discontinue anything before that conversation.
Record the first day of your last menstrual period and your usual cycle length, since both are needed for dating before an ultrasound is available.
Arrange the dating and nuchal translucency ultrasound, usually offered between 11 weeks 2 days and 14 weeks 1 day, and decide in advance whether you want combined or cell-free DNA screening.
Seek same-day assessment for heavy bleeding, one-sided pelvic pain, shoulder-tip pain, fainting, fever above 38 degrees Celsius, or severe persistent vomiting that prevents keeping fluids down.

sections.heading: When It Does Not Go to Plan
sections.body:
Most pregnancy planning guidance implicitly assumes success within a few months, which leaves people unprepared for the two commonest outcomes that are not that: taking longer than expected, and losing a pregnancy. Both are far more usual than public conversation suggests, and both have a defined path forward.

On timing, the benchmark is that about 85 per cent of couples having regular unprotected intercourse conceive within twelve months, and roughly half of the remainder conceive in the following year without treatment. Infertility is conventionally defined as failure to conceive after twelve months, reduced to six months when the female partner is over 35 and to immediate assessment where there is an obvious cause such as absent or very irregular periods, known tubal disease, previous pelvic infection or surgery, endometriosis, chemotherapy exposure, or a known male factor. Waiting the full year in those situations wastes time that is not recoverable.

Initial investigation is straightforward and should proceed in parallel for both partners rather than sequentially. It typically comprises semen analysis, confirmation of ovulation with a mid-luteal progesterone measured about seven days before the expected period, assessment of tubal patency by hysterosalpingography or laparoscopy, a pelvic ultrasound, and hormonal tests including thyroid function and, where polycystic ovary syndrome is suspected, androgens. Treatment depends entirely on the cause: ovulation induction with letrozole or clomifene, surgery for tubal or endometriotic disease, intrauterine insemination, or in vitro fertilisation with or without intracytoplasmic sperm injection. Success rates fall sharply with female age and should be requested as age-specific live-birth rates per cycle started, not as pregnancy rates per embryo transfer, which flatter the figures considerably.

Miscarriage occurs in roughly 10 to 20 per cent of clinically recognised pregnancies and in a much higher proportion of all conceptions, many of which are never detected. Around half to two-thirds result from chromosomal abnormalities in the embryo, which are random events, not consequences of anything the parents did. Lifting, exercise, sex, stress, minor falls and working do not cause miscarriage, and it is worth saying so directly, because unwarranted self-blame is close to universal. Recurrent miscarriage, usually defined as two or three consecutive losses, justifies investigation for antiphospholipid syndrome, uterine structural abnormalities, thyroid disease, poorly controlled diabetes and parental chromosomal rearrangements; even after full investigation, around half of cases have no identified cause, and the prognosis for a subsequent pregnancy remains reasonably good.

Grief after early loss is frequently unrecognised by others, who may not have known about the pregnancy at all. It is a real bereavement, not a disappointment, and the absence of ritual or acknowledgement makes it harder rather than easier. Seeking support is proportionate. So is deciding, after due consideration, to stop trying; that is a legitimate outcome and not a failure of planning.

guides.safetyNote: This guide is general education, not personal medical advice. Pregnancy decisions depend on your individual history, and some situations are emergencies: heavy vaginal bleeding, severe one-sided abdominal or shoulder-tip pain in early pregnancy (possible ectopic pregnancy), a severe headache with visual changes or upper abdominal pain after 20 weeks (possible pre-eclampsia), fever above 38 C, or reduced fetal movement after 28 weeks all warrant urgent assessment rather than waiting. Never start or stop a prescribed medicine on the strength of a written guide.

guides.title: Testicular Self-Examination and Health
guides.summary: How to examine the testicles, what normal anatomy feels like, and what the common lumps, pains and swellings mean, including testicular cancer, torsion and infection, and when a symptom is an emergency rather than something to watch.

sections.heading: Why This Is Worth Knowing
sections.body:
Testicular problems occupy an unusual position in health: they are common, they are easy to detect by hand, several of them are extremely treatable when caught early, one of them destroys an organ within hours if ignored, and almost nobody talks about them. That combination makes basic knowledge unusually valuable. A few minutes of understanding can be the difference between a routine outpatient appointment and a surgical emergency, or between an early-stage cancer with a cure rate above ninety-five per cent and a late-stage one requiring intensive chemotherapy.

Testicular cancer is the headline reason people are told to examine themselves, and it deserves proportionate framing. It is not a common cancer overall, representing roughly one per cent of all cancers in men, with incidence in most Western countries somewhere around six to ten new cases per hundred thousand men per year. But it is the most common solid cancer in men aged roughly fifteen to forty-five, which is precisely the age group least likely to see a doctor about anything. And it is one of oncology's genuine success stories: five-year survival for localised disease exceeds ninety-nine per cent, and even with distant spread survival is around seventy-three per cent, figures transformed by the introduction of cisplatin-based chemotherapy in the late 1970s.

The more common reasons to know your own anatomy are benign. Epididymal cysts, varicoceles, hydroceles and simple sebaceous cysts of the scrotal skin are all frequent, all harmless in themselves, and all capable of causing considerable alarm when discovered unexpectedly. Being able to recognise the normal lumpy structures that everyone has — particularly the epididymis, which is a genuinely lump-like organ sitting on the back of each testicle — prevents a great deal of unnecessary fear.

The urgent reason is testicular torsion. The spermatic cord can twist, cutting off the blood supply, and the testicle begins to die within hours. Salvage rates are around ninety to one hundred per cent if surgery occurs within six hours of onset, fall to roughly fifty per cent by twelve hours, and are around ten per cent or less beyond twenty-four hours. Torsion presents as sudden severe pain, usually with nausea. Anybody who does not know that this is a surgical emergency may wait overnight, and by morning the organ is not salvageable.

A note on evidence and honesty is appropriate at the outset. Formal screening programmes for testicular cancer are not recommended by most national bodies, and some, including the United States Preventive Services Task Force, have concluded that evidence does not support routine self-examination as a population screening measure. That conclusion is about population-level programmes and does not mean the knowledge is useless. Familiarity with your own anatomy and the ability to recognise a change is a reasonable, low-cost thing to have, provided it does not become anxious over-checking.

sections.heading: The Anatomy You Are Feeling
sections.body:
To examine yourself sensibly you need a mental map of what is there, because the scrotum contains several structures that feel quite different from one another and several of them feel, to an unprepared hand, like lumps.

The testicle itself, properly the testis, is an oval organ typically about four to five centimetres long, two to three centimetres wide and three centimetres deep in an adult, with a volume usually between fifteen and twenty-five millilitres. It should feel firm, smooth and uniform, with a consistency often compared to a peeled hard-boiled egg or a firm plum. It is slightly compressible but not soft. There should be no discrete hard nodules on or within it. Mild tenderness to firm squeezing is normal; the testicle is a sensitive organ.

Sitting on the back and upper part of each testicle, and extending down its posterior surface, is the epididymis. This is a single coiled tube some six metres long packed into a structure a few centimetres in size, where sperm mature and are stored. It feels like a soft, slightly irregular, comma-shaped ridge, and it is by far the most common thing mistaken for an abnormal lump. It is supposed to feel lumpy. Learning to identify it, and to recognise that it is separate from the smooth testis in front of it, is the single most useful skill in self-examination.

Running upward from the top of the epididymis is the spermatic cord, containing the vas deferens, blood vessels, lymphatics and nerves. The vas deferens is distinctive: a firm, smooth, mobile tube roughly the thickness of cooked spaghetti, which can be rolled between finger and thumb. Alongside it the pampiniform plexus of veins is normally not palpable, but when dilated it produces a varicocele, classically described as feeling like a bag of worms.

It is entirely normal for the two testicles to differ. One usually hangs lower than the other, most commonly the left, an arrangement thought to reduce compression between the thighs and possibly to aid heat dissipation. A size difference of up to about ten to twenty per cent between the two is within normal variation. The scrotum itself changes markedly with temperature, because the dartos and cremaster muscles contract in cold and relax in warmth, drawing the testicles up tight against the body or letting them hang loose. This is why examination is much easier when warm.

Small structures at the upper pole, the appendix testis and appendix epididymis, are embryological remnants of no function. They matter only because they can twist on their own, producing a painful but far less serious condition than true torsion.

One anatomical detail has outsized clinical importance. Because the testicles form high in the abdomen and only later descend into the scrotum, their blood supply, nerve supply and lymphatic drainage all remain abdominal. Lymph from the testis therefore drains not to the groin nodes, as scrotal skin does, but to nodes deep in the abdomen alongside the aorta. This is why a testicular tumour spreads first to the abdomen, and why the scrotum is never cut to biopsy one.

sections.heading: How To Examine Yourself
sections.body:
Self-examination is simple, takes about two minutes, and is best done once a month. The purpose is not to diagnose anything — that is a clinician's job — but to become so familiar with your own normal that a change is obvious. There is no benefit in doing it more often than monthly, and daily checking is a recognised feature of health anxiety rather than good practice.

Timing matters. Examine during or just after a warm shower or bath, because heat relaxes the cremaster muscle and the scrotal skin, letting the testicles hang loose and making the structures easy to distinguish. In the cold, everything is drawn up tight against the body and the epididymis is pressed against the testis, which makes the examination both harder and more likely to produce a false alarm.

The examination should be gentle throughout. Rolling firmly enough to cause real pain is unnecessary and can cause bruising.
steps: Stand in a warm room or shower, and if possible look first in a mirror at the scrotum for any obvious swelling, asymmetry, redness, or change in the skin. Note that some asymmetry is normal and one side normally hangs lower.
Examine one testicle at a time. Cup it in the palm of one hand and take note of its size and weight; comparing the two sides is one of the more useful things you can do.

Place the thumb on the front of the testicle and the index and middle fingers behind it, then roll it gently between fingers and thumb, working systematically over the whole surface so no area is missed.

Feel for the smooth uniform texture of the body of the testis. You are looking for any hard, pea-sized or larger lump within it, any area that feels distinctly firmer than the rest, or any change in overall size or heaviness.

Find the epididymis, the soft, slightly irregular, comma-shaped structure along the back and upper part of the testicle. Identify it deliberately, so you recognise it as a normal structure rather than a lump.

Trace the spermatic cord upward from the top of the epididymis. Roll the firm, smooth vas deferens between your fingers. Note whether there is any soft, worm-like mass of veins around it, particularly on the left, which is a varicocele.
Repeat the entire process on the other side, and compare. A clear difference in size, weight or firmness that was not there before is worth reporting.

Note anything new: a lump, an ache or heaviness in the scrotum or lower abdomen, a change in size or firmness, or fluid collection. If something has changed, arrange to see a doctor rather than waiting to see whether it resolves.

sections.heading: What Normal Feels Like, and What Does Not
sections.body:
The commonest reason people either panic unnecessarily or fail to act on something real is that they have no baseline for comparison. It is worth being explicit about the distinction between the reassuring findings and the concerning ones, while recognising that no description can substitute for examination by a clinician.

Reassuring characteristics of a lump include being clearly separate from the body of the testicle, being soft or fluid-filled rather than hard, being tender in a way that fits an obvious infection, transilluminating — that is, glowing when a torch is pressed against the scrotum in a dark room, which indicates clear fluid rather than solid tissue — and having been present unchanged for years. The classic benign findings all share the feature of being attached to or above the testis rather than arising from within it.

The concerning pattern is different and worth memorising. A testicular cancer classically presents as a painless, hard lump arising from the body of the testicle itself, firm and irregular, not separable from the testis, not transilluminating, and slowly enlarging. Around seventy to eighty per cent of testicular tumours are painless at presentation, which is exactly the problem: the absence of pain is treated as reassurance when it is nothing of the kind. Other presentations include a general enlargement or change in firmness of one testicle without a discrete lump, a dull ache or sense of heaviness in the scrotum or lower abdomen, or a sudden collection of fluid around the testicle.

Some presentations are misleading. A minority of testicular cancers do cause pain, sometimes because of bleeding into the tumour, and pain therefore does not exclude cancer. A small proportion present first with symptoms of spread rather than a scrotal lump: a lump in the neck from lymph node involvement, back pain from enlarged retroperitoneal nodes, breathlessness or cough from lung deposits, or breast tenderness and enlargement, called gynaecomastia, caused by hormone production by the tumour. A man in his twenties or thirties with unexplained back pain, a supraclavicular node or new gynaecomastia should have his testicles examined.

A change in size without any lump at all is easy to dismiss and should not be. A testicle that has become noticeably larger, heavier or firmer than its partner over weeks to months, or conversely one that has shrunk, is a genuine finding even when nothing discrete can be felt, because a tumour can replace the substance of the organ diffusely rather than forming a distinct nodule.

The honest position on discrimination by feel is that it is imperfect even for experienced clinicians, which is why ultrasound exists. Scrotal ultrasound is quick, painless, involves no radiation, and has a sensitivity approaching one hundred per cent for distinguishing lesions within the testis from those outside it. Anyone who finds something new and cannot confidently identify it as the epididymis should be scanned rather than reassured over the telephone. The correct approach to an uncertain lump is not prolonged self-analysis but a low threshold for getting it imaged.

sections.heading: Testicular Cancer: What It Is and Who Gets It
sections.body:
Testicular cancer arises overwhelmingly from germ cells, the cells that give rise to sperm, and germ cell tumours account for roughly ninety to ninety-five per cent of cases. They divide into two broad groups with important differences. Seminomas, comprising very roughly half of cases, arise from cells resembling primitive germ cells, tend to occur slightly later with a peak in the thirties and forties, grow relatively slowly, and are exceptionally sensitive to radiotherapy. Non-seminomatous germ cell tumours — a group including embryonal carcinoma, yolk sac tumour, choriocarcinoma and teratoma, often mixed together in a single tumour — peak earlier, in the late teens and twenties, and behave more aggressively but respond very well to chemotherapy. The remaining small percentage are sex cord–stromal tumours such as Leydig and Sertoli cell tumours, and lymphoma, which is the commonest testicular malignancy in men over sixty.

The precursor lesion is now well characterised: germ cell neoplasia in situ, formerly called intratubular germ cell neoplasia, is found adjacent to almost all germ cell tumours and is thought to arise during fetal development from a primordial germ cell that fails to differentiate normally. It then remains dormant for one to three decades before progressing. This developmental origin explains much of the epidemiology, including why risk factors act before birth and why the disease peaks in young adulthood.

The dominant risk factor is cryptorchidism, an undescended testis. It increases risk by a factor of roughly four to eight, and the risk applies to both testicles, not only the affected one, which indicates that the underlying problem is a developmental abnormality rather than the anatomical position itself. Orchidopexy, surgical correction, reduces but does not eliminate the risk and is most protective when performed before puberty. Other established factors are a personal history of a germ cell tumour in the other testicle, which carries roughly a two to five per cent risk of a second primary; a family history, with a father or brother affected raising risk perhaps four to eightfold; certain disorders of sex development; infertility and poor semen quality; and HIV infection for seminoma.

Ethnicity and geography show a striking and unexplained pattern. Incidence is highest in Northern Europe, particularly Denmark, Norway and Switzerland, and in populations of European descent, and is several times lower in men of African and Asian descent. Incidence has roughly doubled in many Western countries over the past half-century, an increase too rapid to be genetic, which has driven hypotheses about prenatal endocrine-disrupting chemical exposure as part of a proposed testicular dysgenesis syndrome linking cryptorchidism, hypospadias, poor semen quality and cancer. This remains a plausible but unproven hypothesis. Notably, neither trauma nor vasectomy nor sexual activity causes testicular cancer; trauma merely draws attention to a lump already present.

sections.heading: Diagnosis, Staging and Tumour Markers
sections.body:
When a suspicious testicular mass is found, the diagnostic pathway is well established and moves quickly. The first investigation is a scrotal ultrasound with a high-frequency probe, typically seven to fourteen megahertz. This distinguishes an intratesticular lesion, which must be assumed malignant until proved otherwise, from an extratesticular one, which is almost always benign. It also assesses the opposite testicle. Ultrasound is close to definitive for localisation and is available within days in most systems.

Blood is then taken for serum tumour markers, which are unusually useful in this disease. Alpha-fetoprotein is produced by yolk sac elements and is raised in a substantial proportion of non-seminomatous tumours; crucially, a raised alpha-fetoprotein essentially excludes pure seminoma, since seminomas do not produce it. Beta human chorionic gonadotrophin, the same hormone measured in pregnancy tests, is produced by trophoblastic elements and is raised in most choriocarcinomas, many other non-seminomas, and about fifteen to twenty per cent of seminomas. Lactate dehydrogenase is non-specific but correlates with tumour bulk and is used in prognostic staging. Markers are measured before surgery, then again afterwards to confirm they fall along their expected half-lives — roughly five to seven days for alpha-fetoprotein and one to three days for beta-hCG. Failure to fall appropriately indicates residual disease.

A crucial point of surgical principle: unlike almost every other cancer, testicular tumours are not biopsied through the scrotum. A needle or incision through the scrotal skin risks seeding tumour into a different lymphatic drainage territory, converting a straightforward problem into a complicated one. Instead the standard procedure is radical inguinal orchidectomy, in which the testicle and spermatic cord are removed through an incision in the groin with the cord clamped early. This is both the definitive diagnostic test and the first stage of treatment. In selected cases with small lesions, testis-sparing surgery is considered, particularly in men with a single testicle.

Staging is completed with computed tomography of the chest, abdomen and pelvis, because these tumours spread first to the retroperitoneal lymph nodes along the path of embryological descent, and later to lungs, liver, brain and bone. The staging system combines anatomical extent with post-orchidectomy marker levels, and the International Germ Cell Cancer Collaborative Group classification divides metastatic disease into good, intermediate and poor prognosis groups, with five-year survival of roughly ninety, eighty and fifty per cent respectively.

Because the opposite testicle carries a small but real risk of a second primary tumour, some centres biopsy it at the time of surgery in men with recognised risk factors such as a history of undescended testis or a small remaining testicular volume, though practice varies between countries and the benefit is debated.

One practical matter should be raised before any treatment begins: sperm banking. Chemotherapy, radiotherapy and retroperitoneal surgery can all impair fertility, and many men already have reduced sperm counts at diagnosis. Semen cryopreservation should be offered and arranged before treatment starts, since it cannot be done retrospectively.

sections.heading: Treatment and Outcomes for Testicular Cancer
sections.body:
Treatment begins with radical inguinal orchidectomy, which removes the primary tumour and establishes the histological diagnosis. What follows depends on the cell type, the stage and the tumour marker levels, and the modern emphasis is on giving the least treatment that achieves cure, because these patients are young and will live for decades with whatever side effects the treatment causes.

For stage I seminoma confined to the testis, three options exist with essentially identical survival above ninety-nine per cent: active surveillance with regular imaging and markers, a single cycle of carboplatin chemotherapy, or adjuvant radiotherapy to the para-aortic nodes. Surveillance has become the preferred approach in most centres, because roughly eighty to eighty-five per cent of these men are already cured by surgery alone, and treating everyone exposes the majority to unnecessary toxicity. Those who relapse are treated then, with the same excellent outcomes. Radiotherapy has fallen out of favour largely because of a documented increase in second malignancies decades later.

For stage I non-seminoma, the options are surveillance or one to two cycles of the BEP regimen — bleomycin, etoposide and cisplatin. Risk is stratified largely by whether lymphovascular invasion is present in the specimen, which roughly doubles the relapse rate from about fifteen to fifty per cent. Retroperitoneal lymph node dissection remains an option in some centres.

Metastatic disease is treated with combination chemotherapy, and this is where the modern history of the disease is remarkable. Before the mid-1970s, metastatic testicular cancer was largely fatal. The introduction of cisplatin, developed after Barnett Rosenberg's serendipitous 1965 observation that platinum electrodes inhibited bacterial cell division, and its incorporation into combination regimens by Lawrence Einhorn at Indiana University from 1974, transformed cure rates from around ten per cent to around eighty per cent within a few years. It remains one of the most dramatic single advances in the history of oncology. Typically three to four cycles of BEP are given, with residual masses resected surgically afterwards, since residual teratoma is chemoresistant and must be removed.

The late effects deserve honest mention because the patients are young. Cisplatin causes cumulative hearing loss and tinnitus, peripheral neuropathy, and kidney impairment; bleomycin can cause pulmonary fibrosis, and patients are advised to inform anaesthetists because high inspired oxygen can precipitate lung injury. There is an increased long-term risk of cardiovascular disease, metabolic syndrome, hypogonadism requiring testosterone replacement, and second cancers. Around twenty to thirty per cent of men have reduced fertility afterwards, though many recover over two to three years.

Loss of one testicle does not impair sexual function or fertility in most men, since the remaining testis compensates. A silicone prosthesis can be implanted at the time of surgery or later for cosmetic and psychological reasons, and it is worth asking about beforehand.

sections.heading: Testicular Torsion: The True Emergency
sections.body:
Testicular torsion is the one scrotal condition where minutes genuinely count, and it is the reason nobody should ever be advised to wait and see with sudden severe testicular pain.

The mechanism is mechanical. The testis normally has a broad posterior attachment to the scrotal wall. In perhaps one in a hundred and twenty-five males there is an anatomical variant called the bell clapper deformity, in which the tunica vaginalis surrounds the testis completely and it hangs freely on the cord like a clapper in a bell, able to rotate. When it twists, typically through one hundred and eighty to seven hundred and twenty degrees, it first occludes the thin-walled veins, causing congestion and swelling, which then compresses the arteries and cuts off arterial supply. The result is ischaemia and progressive infarction of the testicular tissue. The deformity is usually bilateral, which is why surgery fixes both sides.

Torsion has two incidence peaks: the neonatal period, and puberty through the early twenties, with the greatest frequency around age thirteen to sixteen. It often occurs at night or on waking, sometimes after exercise or minor trauma, and sometimes with no trigger at all.

The presentation is characteristic. Pain is sudden in onset, severe, and usually one-sided, frequently accompanied by nausea and vomiting, which is a useful discriminator because infection rarely causes prompt vomiting. The affected testicle is exquisitely tender, may be swollen, sits higher than the other and may lie horizontally rather than vertically. The cremasteric reflex — the testicle rising when the inner thigh is stroked — is typically absent on the affected side, and lifting the testicle does not relieve pain, in contrast to epididymitis where it often does. Some men describe previous brief episodes of similar pain that resolved spontaneously, which represents intermittent torsion and detorsion and is itself a reason for urgent referral.

The time course is the critical fact. Salvage rates approach ninety to one hundred per cent within six hours of onset, fall to around fifty per cent by twelve hours, and to ten per cent or lower beyond twenty-four hours. Beyond that the testis is usually non-viable and is removed. Because of this, torsion is a clinical diagnosis leading to immediate surgical exploration; waiting for an ultrasound must not delay theatre, and a normal Doppler scan does not exclude torsion, since flow may be preserved in partial or intermittent cases.

Treatment is urgent scrotal exploration, untwisting the cord, assessing viability, and fixing both testicles to the scrotal wall with sutures, a procedure called bilateral orchidopexy. If the testis is dead it is removed to prevent later problems.

The practical instruction is unambiguous: sudden severe testicular pain, particularly in a boy or young man, particularly with nausea, means going to an emergency department immediately, at whatever hour it happens. Do not take a painkiller and go back to bed.

sections.heading: Common Benign Lumps and Swellings
sections.body:
Most scrotal lumps are not cancer, and knowing the common benign entities removes a great deal of unnecessary fear while making it easier to recognise the pattern that is not benign.

An epididymal cyst, and its close relative the spermatocele which contains sperm-laden fluid, is a smooth, round, fluid-filled swelling arising from the epididymis, most often at its head above and behind the testicle. It is separate from the testis, transilluminates brightly, is usually painless, and may be a few millimetres or several centimetres across. They are extremely common, found in perhaps a third of men on ultrasound, and increase with age. No treatment is needed unless they become large or uncomfortable, and surgery carries a small risk of damaging the epididymis and impairing fertility, so it is generally avoided in men who want children.

A hydrocele is a collection of clear fluid between the layers of the tunica vaginalis surrounding the testis. It presents as a soft, non-tender swelling that surrounds the testicle rather than sitting beside it, transilluminates well, and can become large enough to be a nuisance. Most in adults are idiopathic, but a hydrocele that appears suddenly, particularly in a young man, may be reactive to an underlying tumour or infection, and the testis must be imaged to be sure it is normal. Infantile hydroceles usually resolve spontaneously in the first year or two.

A varicocele is a dilated pampiniform venous plexus, classically described as feeling like a bag of worms above and around the testicle, more prominent on standing and when bearing down, and often disappearing when lying flat. Roughly fifteen per cent of men have one. Around eighty to ninety per cent occur on the left, because the left testicular vein drains at a right angle into the left renal vein rather than obliquely into the vena cava, giving a longer column of blood and higher pressure. Varicoceles are associated with impaired sperm quality and modest testicular atrophy and are found in a substantial minority of men presenting with infertility. One warning: a varicocele that appears suddenly, is right-sided, or does not decompress on lying down can indicate obstruction of the venous drainage by an abdominal mass, including a kidney tumour, and warrants imaging.

Other benign findings include sebaceous cysts in the scrotal skin, which are in the skin itself and move with it; inguinal hernias, where bowel descends into the scrotum, producing a swelling that you cannot get above with your fingers and that may reduce when lying down; and simple scrotal oedema in heart, liver or kidney failure. Small calcifications and microlithiasis are frequently found incidentally on ultrasound and are generally of little consequence on their own.

sections.heading: Infections: Epididymitis, Orchitis and Their Causes
sections.body:
Infection is the commonest cause of a painful, swollen testicle in adults, and distinguishing it from torsion is one of the more consequential judgements in acute care.

Epididymitis is inflammation of the epididymis, and it is the usual pattern. The onset is gradual over hours to days rather than sudden, the pain begins at the back of the testicle where the epididymis sits and spreads forward, and there is often fever, urinary symptoms such as burning or frequency, or urethral discharge. The scrotum becomes red, hot and swollen. Classically, lifting the testicle relieves the pain — Prehn's sign — whereas in torsion it does not, though this sign is unreliable enough that it must never be used to rule out torsion. The cremasteric reflex is usually preserved.

The causative organism depends strongly on age and sexual history, and this determines treatment. In sexually active men under about thirty-five, the usual causes are the sexually transmitted organisms Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae, and treatment must cover both, typically with an intramuscular cephalosporin plus doxycycline, along with partner notification and treatment. In older men, and in those with urinary tract abnormalities or after instrumentation, the usual organisms are coliforms such as Escherichia coli arising from the urinary tract, treated with a quinolone or another agent guided by urine culture. In men who practise insertive anal intercourse, enteric organisms should also be covered.

Orchitis, inflammation of the testis itself, most often occurs as an extension of epididymitis, giving epididymo-orchitis. Isolated orchitis is characteristically viral, and mumps is the classic cause: it occurs in roughly twenty to thirty per cent of post-pubertal males with mumps, usually four to eight days after the parotid swelling, is bilateral in around fifteen to thirty per cent of those, and can cause permanent testicular atrophy and impaired fertility, though outright sterility is uncommon. This is a preventable disease, and the measles-mumps-rubella vaccine is the reason it is now rare where uptake is high; mumps orchitis reappears reliably in communities where vaccination coverage falls.

Two less common but important causes should be mentioned. Tuberculous epididymitis presents insidiously over weeks with a firm, relatively painless swelling and sometimes a discharging sinus, and remains a real consideration where tuberculosis is endemic. And the anti-arrhythmic drug amiodarone causes a sterile, non-infective epididymitis that resolves on dose reduction.

Treatment of bacterial infection is antibiotics for ten to fourteen days, together with rest, scrotal elevation and support, ice, and anti-inflammatory analgesia. Symptoms should begin improving within two to three days; failure to improve raises the possibility of abscess formation, an incorrect organism, or a missed alternative diagnosis such as torsion or tumour. A residual firm swelling that persists for weeks after infection should be scanned, since an underlying tumour can present with reactive inflammation. Chronic epididymitis, lasting beyond three months, is a distinct and frustrating condition that often has no identifiable infective cause and responds poorly to further antibiotics.

sections.heading: Trauma, Everyday Injury and Protection
sections.body:
The testicles are poorly protected by anatomy, being suspended outside the body wall, and they are richly supplied with autonomic nerve fibres, which is why even minor trauma produces pain out of all proportion to the injury, along with nausea and a sickening abdominal sensation. The nerve supply arises from the tenth thoracic spinal segment, the same level as much of the gut, which is why testicular pain is felt in the lower abdomen and why testicular problems are sometimes mistaken for abdominal ones and vice versa.

Most blunt trauma is minor. Pain that peaks quickly and then settles substantially over ten to sixty minutes, with no significant swelling or bruising, requires nothing more than rest, support, ice for twenty minutes at a time and simple analgesia. What matters is knowing which injuries are not minor. Pain that does not settle, marked or progressive swelling, extensive bruising of the scrotum, inability to feel the outline of the testicle because of surrounding blood, nausea and vomiting that persists, difficulty passing urine, or blood in the urine all warrant urgent assessment.

Testicular rupture is the injury that must not be missed. A sufficiently forceful blow can tear the tough fibrous capsule, the tunica albuginea, allowing the seminiferous tubules to extrude. It is diagnosed on ultrasound and requires surgical repair, and the salvage rate is around eighty to ninety per cent when operated within seventy-two hours, falling substantially thereafter. A large haematocele — a collection of blood around the testis — may also require drainage. Trauma can also precipitate torsion, so severe pain after a blow that does not settle should be treated as a possible torsion.

An important and frequently misunderstood point: trauma does not cause testicular cancer. What it does is prompt examination, and a proportion of tumours are found this way, giving rise to a false association. A lump found after an injury should still be investigated as a lump.

Protection is straightforward and underused. A properly fitted hard cup worn in a supportive jockstrap or compression short is standard in cricket, baseball, hockey, martial arts, lacrosse, motorsport and boxing, and it prevents the great majority of serious injuries in those sports. Cups should be sized correctly, since an ill-fitting one is uncomfortable and often abandoned. Soft compression shorts alone provide support but little impact protection.

Two further everyday matters are worth noting. Prolonged heat, from hot tubs, saunas, heated seats or laptops resting on the lap, temporarily depresses sperm production, because the testicles function best at roughly two to four degrees Celsius below core body temperature; the effect is reversible over about three months, the length of a spermatogenesis cycle. And tight underwear has a small measurable effect on sperm parameters in some studies, though the clinical significance for most men is minor.

sections.heading: Pain Without a Lump: Causes and Approach
sections.body:
Testicular pain without an obvious lump is a common and often frustrating presentation, and the differential is broad because the region receives referred pain from several other structures.

The first task is always to exclude the emergencies. Sudden severe pain of recent onset is torsion until proved otherwise. Torsion of a testicular appendage — one of the small embryological remnants at the upper pole — produces a similar but usually milder picture, most often in boys aged seven to fourteen, sometimes with a characteristic small blue dot visible through the scrotal skin at the upper pole. It is self-limiting and treated with analgesia, but distinguishing it from true torsion reliably enough to avoid surgery is often not possible, so exploration is common.

Referred pain is the commonest cause of testicular ache with a normal examination. A ureteric stone passing down the lower ureter refers pain to the ipsilateral testicle with great reliability, because the nerve supply is shared; the pain is usually colicky, severe, associated with loin pain and often blood in the urine. An inguinal hernia can cause dragging discomfort. Nerve entrapment or irritation of the ilioinguinal or genitofemoral nerve, sometimes following hernia repair, causes a persistent burning or neuralgic pain. Lumbar spine pathology can refer to the groin. Rarely, an abdominal aortic aneurysm or retroperitoneal mass presents this way.

Chronic scrotal pain, defined as intermittent or constant pain lasting three months or more that interferes with daily life, affects a significant number of men and is genuinely difficult. Recognised causes include post-vasectomy pain syndrome, which occurs in perhaps one to two per cent of men after vasectomy in a form severe enough to affect quality of life; varicocele; chronic epididymitis; and a large residual group with no identifiable cause, sometimes termed idiopathic chronic orchialgia. The mechanism in many of these appears to involve peripheral and central nerve sensitisation rather than ongoing tissue damage, which is why repeated courses of antibiotics do not help and why treatments aimed at nerves, including gabapentinoids, tricyclic antidepressants, nerve blocks and in selected cases microsurgical denervation of the spermatic cord, are used instead.

The practical approach is to have the emergencies excluded promptly, to have a urine test and an ultrasound to identify treatable structural causes, and then, if nothing is found, to resist the temptation to pursue ever more investigations. Repeated normal scans do not become more reassuring, and prolonged uncertainty tends to worsen the pain through anxiety and hypervigilance. Multidisciplinary chronic pain management, including physiotherapy of the pelvic floor and psychological support, has better evidence than repeated surgery, and men should be counselled that orchidectomy for chronic pain frequently fails to relieve it.

sections.heading: The Testicle's Two Jobs: Sperm and Hormones
sections.body:
Understanding what the testicle does makes it easier to understand what goes wrong. It performs two quite separate functions in two different compartments.

Inside the seminiferous tubules, which make up the bulk of the organ, spermatogenesis occurs. Germ cells divide and differentiate, supported physically and nutritionally by Sertoli cells, which also form the blood–testis barrier isolating developing sperm from the immune system. The full cycle from spermatogonium to mature spermatozoon takes approximately seventy-four days, plus a further ten to fourteen days of maturation and transit through the epididymis. This roughly three-month lag has an important practical consequence: any insult — a fever, an illness, a heat exposure, a drug — shows up in a semen analysis two to three months later, not immediately, and recovery takes a similar time. It also means a single abnormal semen analysis means little and should always be repeated.

Between the tubules lie the Leydig cells, which produce testosterone under the control of luteinising hormone from the pituitary. Sertoli cell function is driven by follicle-stimulating hormone, and inhibin B secreted by Sertoli cells feeds back to suppress it. This hypothalamic–pituitary–gonadal axis is the reason blood tests can localise a problem: high FSH and LH with low testosterone indicate primary testicular failure, whereas low or inappropriately normal gonadotrophins with low testosterone point to a pituitary or hypothalamic cause.

Testosterone does far more than drive libido. It maintains muscle mass and bone density, red blood cell production, mood and cognition, and body hair. Symptoms of deficiency — fatigue, low mood, reduced libido, erectile difficulty, loss of morning erections, poor concentration, reduced muscle and increased fat, and eventually osteoporosis — are non-specific and easily attributed to age or stress. Diagnosis requires a morning blood sample, ideally two on separate days, because testosterone follows a diurnal rhythm peaking in the early morning.

An important and frequently missed cause of low testosterone is anabolic steroid use. Exogenous testosterone or its analogues suppress the axis, shrinking the testicles and shutting down natural production and sperm output, sometimes with prolonged or incomplete recovery after stopping. The same is true of prescribed testosterone replacement, which is an effective contraceptive-like suppressor of spermatogenesis and should not be given to a man who wants children in the near future; alternatives such as human chorionic gonadotrophin or clomiphene preserve fertility.

Other reversible causes of impaired sperm production worth knowing are varicocele, obesity, heavy alcohol use, smoking, cannabis, certain medications including sulfasalazine and some chemotherapy, untreated diabetes, and heat exposure. Around fifteen per cent of couples experience infertility and a male factor contributes in roughly half of those cases, so semen analysis should be part of the early assessment rather than an afterthought.

sections.heading: Development, Childhood and the Undescended Testis
sections.body:
The testicles develop inside the abdomen near the kidneys and descend through the inguinal canal into the scrotum during the last months of gestation, generally between about twenty-eight and forty weeks. This journey explains several otherwise puzzling facts: why the blood supply and lymphatic drainage of the testis are abdominal rather than scrotal, why testicular cancer spreads first to lymph nodes deep in the abdomen rather than to the groin, and why the testis can drag a pouch of peritoneum with it that later becomes a hernia or hydrocele.

Cryptorchidism, failure of descent, affects roughly three per cent of full-term male infants and up to thirty per cent of premature ones, reflecting the timing of descent. Many descend spontaneously in the first three to six months, after which spontaneous descent is unlikely. Current guidance is therefore to refer by six months of corrected age and to operate, with orchidopexy bringing the testis into the scrotum and fixing it there, between about six and eighteen months. The rationale is twofold: preserving fertility, since the higher temperature inside the body damages germ cells progressively, and reducing cancer risk while making the testis examinable. Orchidopexy reduces but does not abolish the elevated cancer risk, and men who had the operation should be taught self-examination, since their lifetime risk remains several times the background rate.

A retractile testis must be distinguished from a truly undescended one. An overactive cremasteric reflex can pull a normal testis up into the groin, particularly in cold or when a child is anxious, but it can be gently brought down into the scrotum and stays there briefly. This requires monitoring rather than surgery, though a minority later become genuinely ascended and need operating on.

Other paediatric matters recur. Hydroceles in infants are common, usually resolve by one to two years, and need surgery only if persistent or associated with a hernia. Torsion in the neonate is usually extravaginal, often occurs before or during birth, and the testis is rarely salvageable. In older boys, torsion of the appendix testis is far more common than true torsion but cannot always be distinguished from it.

Puberty brings its own concerns. Testicular enlargement to above about four millilitres in volume is the first physical sign of puberty in boys, typically between about nine and fourteen years. Gynaecomastia, breast tissue development, occurs in roughly half of adolescent boys, is usually transient and resolves within a couple of years; persistent, rapidly progressive or unilateral gynaecomastia, particularly with a testicular lump, warrants investigation because some testicular tumours secrete hormones. Adolescents should be taught self-examination once puberty is established, since this is the age group in which testicular cancer will eventually appear.

sections.heading: Delay, Embarrassment and Actually Getting Seen
sections.body:
One of the best-documented facts about testicular disease is that men delay seeking help, and the delay causes real harm. Studies of testicular cancer presentation have repeatedly found median patient delays measured in weeks to months, with a substantial minority waiting six months or more from noticing a lump to seeing a doctor. Since these tumours can double in volume in as little as ten to thirty days, particularly the non-seminomatous types, a delay of three months can be the difference between disease confined to the testis and disease in the lungs, and hence between surgery alone and months of chemotherapy.

The reasons for delay are consistent and understandable. Embarrassment about the anatomy and about being examined. The assumption that a painless lump cannot be serious, which is exactly backwards for this disease. Fear of what will be found, and a preference for not knowing. Fear of losing a testicle and what that will mean for sexual function and identity. A general reluctance among young men to consult doctors at all, reinforced by working patterns and by a cultural expectation of stoicism. And, not infrequently, an initial misdiagnosis: a proportion of men are treated for epididymitis with antibiotics and only referred when the swelling fails to settle, which is why persistent symptoms after treatment must be re-examined and scanned rather than given a second course.

Several things help. Knowing that examination is brief, that clinicians examine testicles routinely and find nothing remarkable about it, and that the initial investigation is an ultrasound rather than anything invasive removes much of the anticipatory dread. Knowing that the overwhelming majority of lumps turn out to be benign makes it easier to go and find out. Knowing that losing one testicle does not impair erections, ejaculation, testosterone levels or fertility in most men — the remaining testis compensates — addresses the fear that most often drives avoidance, as does knowing that a prosthesis can be fitted.

Practical measures make a difference too. Ask for a specific appointment for a scrotal lump rather than mentioning it at the end of an appointment about something else. Say plainly at the start what the concern is, because time is short and this should not be the last item raised. Ask for an ultrasound if one is not offered and the lump cannot be confidently identified as a normal structure. Take someone with you if it helps. If you are told it is nothing and it does not settle within a couple of weeks, go back; persistence is reasonable and diagnosis is genuinely difficult by feel alone.

Finally, if you find something in a partner, a friend or a son, say so. A significant number of testicular cancers are found by partners rather than by the man himself.

sections.heading: Limits, Uncertainty and When To Act
sections.body:
A guide of this kind should be clear about what it cannot do, because false confidence in either direction causes harm.

Self-examination cannot diagnose anything. It can only detect change, and its value depends entirely on acting on what it finds. It also has real limitations: small tumours deep within the testis may not be palpable, benign lumps vastly outnumber malignant ones, and even experienced clinicians cannot reliably distinguish them by feel. This is why major bodies including the United States Preventive Services Task Force have concluded that evidence is insufficient to recommend routine self-examination as a population screening programme, a position that is often reported misleadingly as advice not to bother. The honest reading is narrower: there is no trial evidence that a national self-examination programme reduces mortality, partly because outcomes are already so good. Familiarity with your own body remains sensible, inexpensive and harmless, provided it does not become compulsive.

Anxiety cuts both ways. Repeated daily checking, repeated requests for scans and prolonged internet searching are recognised features of health anxiety and make people feel worse rather than safer. If checking has become frequent, distressing or hard to stop, that is itself worth raising with a doctor, and it responds well to treatment. Monthly is enough.

Uncertainty is real in several places and should be acknowledged. The cause of rising testicular cancer incidence in Western countries is not established. The optimal management of small incidental findings such as microlithiasis is debated. Chronic scrotal pain frequently has no identifiable cause and no reliably effective treatment. The long-term consequences of testosterone replacement therapy on cardiovascular risk remain contested. Anyone presenting these as settled is overstating the evidence.

What is not uncertain is the action list, and it is short. Sudden severe testicular pain, particularly with nausea or vomiting, means going to an emergency department immediately, at any hour, without waiting to see if it eases: this is torsion until proved otherwise and the organ is lost in hours. A new hard lump within the body of the testicle, painless or not, means an urgent appointment and an ultrasound, not a period of watchful waiting. A testicle that has changed in size, weight or firmness, or a new dull ache or heaviness in the scrotum or lower abdomen, means the same. A swollen, red, painful scrotum with fever or urinary symptoms needs same-day assessment for infection, and if it does not improve within two to three days of antibiotics, re-assessment and imaging.

Add to that list the less obvious presentations: unexplained back pain, a neck lump, breathlessness or new breast tenderness in a young man are all reasons to have the testicles examined. And a lump found after an injury is still a lump.

guides.safetyNote: Sudden severe testicular pain, especially with nausea or vomiting, is a surgical emergency: go to an emergency department immediately, since a twisted testicle is usually lost within about six to twelve hours. Any new hard lump in the body of a testicle needs urgent medical assessment and an ultrasound, even if it is completely painless. This guide is general information and does not replace examination by a clinician.

guides.title: Male Infertility
guides.summary: How sperm are made, transported and delivered, why that process fails, and how male infertility is investigated and treated: semen analysis and what its numbers mean, hormonal, testicular, genetic and obstructive causes, lifestyle and toxic exposures, and the full range of medical, surgical and assisted-reproduction options along with their honest success rates and limits.

sections.heading: What Male Infertility Is and How Common It Is
sections.body:
Infertility is defined clinically as the failure to achieve a pregnancy after twelve months of regular, unprotected intercourse, which in practice means roughly two to three times a week without contraception and without timing intercourse to ovulation. The twelve-month threshold is not arbitrary. Among couples with no fertility problem at all, about 25 per cent conceive in the first month, about 60 per cent within six months, 85 per cent within a year and 92 per cent within two years. Human reproduction is inefficient month by month, so a couple who have tried for four months and failed are usually simply unlucky rather than infertile. The threshold drops to six months when the female partner is over 35, because the loss of egg quality with age makes delay itself costly.

Infertility affects roughly one couple in seven, or about 15 per cent, in countries where it has been carefully measured. The critical and widely misunderstood fact is how often the male partner is involved. A male factor is the sole cause in approximately 20 to 30 per cent of cases, and contributes alongside a female factor in a further 20 to 30 per cent. Taken together, something about the man is part of the problem in roughly half of all infertile couples. This matters because the historical and cultural default in most of the world has been to investigate the woman first and most thoroughly, subjecting her to invasive tests while the man's contribution is assessed late or not at all. A semen analysis is cheap, non-invasive and can be done in a week. It should be among the first investigations in every couple, not the last.

The distinction between sterility and subfertility is worth holding onto. True sterility, meaning a zero probability of natural conception, is uncommon; it applies to men producing no sperm at all, men with both vasa deferentia absent or blocked, and a few genetic conditions. Far more men are subfertile: their chance of conceiving in any given month is reduced, perhaps from 20 per cent to 5 or 2 per cent, but it is not zero. Such couples often do conceive, simply more slowly, and many of the treatments described in fertility medicine work by nudging a low monthly probability upward rather than by curing anything.

There is also a broader significance. Semen quality is emerging as a general marker of male health. Men with markedly abnormal semen parameters have measurably higher rates of testicular cancer, cardiovascular disease, metabolic syndrome and, in several large cohort studies, higher all-cause mortality over subsequent decades. A fertility evaluation is therefore sometimes the first serious medical assessment a man in his thirties has ever had, and it occasionally uncovers an underlying disorder, from a pituitary tumour to a testicular tumour to undiagnosed diabetes, that has nothing to do with wanting a child.

sections.heading: The Anatomy of Male Reproduction
sections.body:
The male reproductive tract is a factory, a maturation line, a storage depot and a delivery system, and a fault anywhere along it produces the same end result. Understanding where each part sits and what it does makes the causes of infertility far easier to organise.

The testes are paired ovoid organs, normally 4 to 5 centimetres long and 15 to 25 millilitres in volume in an adult, hanging in the scrotum outside the body cavity. That external position is not an accident of design but a functional requirement: sperm production works properly only at about 2 to 4 degrees Celsius below core body temperature, around 34 to 35 degrees rather than 37. The scrotum maintains this with a countercurrent heat exchanger in the spermatic cord, where the warm arterial blood entering the testis is cooled by the venous plexus draining it, and with the cremaster and dartos muscles that draw the testes closer to the body in cold and let them hang in heat.

Inside each testis lie roughly 250 to 400 metres of tightly coiled seminiferous tubules, and it is within their walls that sperm are manufactured. These tubules make up perhaps 80 to 90 per cent of testicular volume, which is why measured testis size is a genuinely informative clinical sign: small testes usually mean a small sperm-producing compartment. Between the tubules sit the Leydig cells, which make testosterone. Within the tubule walls, the large Sertoli cells nurse the developing sperm and form the blood-testis barrier, a sealed layer of tight junctions that isolates maturing sperm from the bloodstream and from the immune system.

Sperm leaving the tubules pass into the rete testis, then through about a dozen efferent ductules into the epididymis, a single coiled tube 4 to 6 metres long folded into a structure a few centimetres in length that caps the back of the testis. From the tail of the epididymis the vas deferens, a thick muscular tube some 30 to 45 centimetres long, ascends in the spermatic cord, passes through the inguinal canal into the pelvis, and joins the duct of the seminal vesicle to form the ejaculatory duct, which opens into the prostatic urethra.

Three accessory glands supply the fluid. The seminal vesicles contribute roughly 65 to 75 per cent of ejaculate volume, an alkaline, fructose-rich secretion that fuels sperm and buffers vaginal acidity. The prostate contributes about 20 to 30 per cent, including zinc, citrate and the enzymes that liquefy the coagulated ejaculate. The bulbourethral glands add a small pre-ejaculatory volume that lubricates and neutralises residual urine. Sperm themselves make up well under 5 per cent of the volume, a fact that explains why a normal-looking ejaculate tells you nothing at all about whether it contains sperm.

sections.heading: Spermatogenesis: How Sperm Are Made
sections.body:
Spermatogenesis is the continuous conversion of a stem cell into a motile, genetically haploid delivery vehicle, and it is among the most productive processes in human biology. A healthy adult male manufactures on the order of 100 to 200 million sperm per day, roughly 1,000 to 1,500 per second, sustained for decades. The whole cycle takes approximately 64 to 74 days from stem cell to sperm released into the tubule lumen, with a further 10 to 14 days spent maturing in the epididymis. That total of about 3 months is the single most useful number in the whole subject, because it dictates that any insult, a fever, a course of chemotherapy, a period of heavy drinking, shows up in the semen roughly 2 to 3 months later, and that any improvement takes at least that long to appear.

The process runs in three phases. In the proliferative phase, spermatogonia sitting on the basement membrane of the seminiferous tubule divide by mitosis. Some daughter cells remain as stem cells, preserving the population indefinitely; others commit to becoming sperm. In the meiotic phase, a committed cell becomes a primary spermatocyte and undergoes the two divisions of meiosis, halving the chromosome number from 46 to 23 and shuffling the parental chromosomes by crossing over, so that each resulting spermatid carries a genetically unique haploid set. In the third phase, spermiogenesis, the round spermatid is remodelled without further division into the recognisable spermatozoon.

That remodelling is dramatic. The Golgi apparatus flattens over the front of the nucleus to become the acrosome, a cap containing the hydrolytic enzymes that will later digest a path through the egg's outer coats. The nucleus condenses to perhaps a twentieth of its former volume as the ordinary histone proteins packaging the DNA are replaced first by transition proteins and then by protamines, small arginine-rich proteins that wind the DNA into a crystalline, almost inert state. Mitochondria migrate to form a helical sheath around the base of the tail, supplying the energy for swimming. A flagellum grows from a centriole, built on the universal nine-plus-two arrangement of microtubule doublets. Finally most of the remaining cytoplasm is stripped away and phagocytosed by Sertoli cells as a residual body.

Two consequences of this design matter clinically. First, the mature sperm is transcriptionally silent, its DNA locked in protamines and its cytoplasm nearly gone, so it cannot repair damage. Damage accumulated during or after spermiogenesis is carried into the egg. Second, the cell has almost no antioxidant capacity left, having discarded the cytoplasm that would contain it, while its membrane is unusually rich in polyunsaturated fatty acids that are chemically vulnerable to oxidation. Sperm are therefore exquisitely sensitive to oxidative stress, a theme that recurs throughout the causes of male infertility.

sections.heading: The Hormonal Control Loop
sections.body:
Sperm production is governed by a three-storey feedback system running between the hypothalamus, the pituitary gland and the testis, known as the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis. Grasping it explains both a large class of causes and the logic of most drug treatments.

At the top, neurones in the hypothalamus release gonadotrophin-releasing hormone, GnRH, not continuously but in pulses roughly every 90 to 120 minutes. The pulsatility is essential rather than incidental: continuous exposure to GnRH paradoxically shuts the system down, which is precisely how GnRH agonist drugs are used to suppress testosterone in prostate cancer. Each pulse reaches the anterior pituitary through a short private circulation, the hypophyseal portal system, and triggers release of two gonadotrophins.

Luteinising hormone, LH, acts on the Leydig cells between the tubules, driving them to convert cholesterol into testosterone. The concentration of testosterone achieved inside the testis is extraordinary, roughly 50 to 100 times the level in the bloodstream, and this intratesticular testosterone is indispensable for sperm production. Follicle-stimulating hormone, FSH, acts instead on the Sertoli cells, supporting their nursing function and the survival of developing germ cells. Broadly, LH sustains the hormonal environment and FSH sustains the cellular support, and both are needed.

The loop closes through two negative feedback signals. Testosterone, and the oestradiol made from it by the enzyme aromatase in fat and other tissues, feed back on the hypothalamus and pituitary to suppress GnRH and LH. The Sertoli cells separately secrete inhibin B, a peptide that selectively suppresses FSH. Inhibin B is therefore a fairly direct blood marker of Sertoli cell mass and spermatogenic activity, and it falls when the germinal epithelium is damaged.

This structure makes hormone measurements diagnostically powerful, because the pattern rather than any single value identifies where the fault lies. If FSH and LH are high while testosterone is low or low-normal, the pituitary is shouting at a testis that cannot respond: the problem is primary testicular failure, called hypergonadotrophic hypogonadism. If FSH and LH are low and testosterone is also low, the testis is never receiving its instructions, and the fault lies above it in the pituitary or hypothalamus, called hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism. If FSH is elevated but testosterone and LH are normal, there is isolated damage to the germinal epithelium with intact Leydig cells, a common finding in men with poor sperm counts. Normal FSH with azoospermia points strongly toward obstruction rather than failure of production.

The most clinically important practical consequence concerns exogenous testosterone. Taking testosterone, whether prescribed for hypogonadism or taken as an anabolic steroid, raises blood levels and therefore suppresses GnRH, LH and FSH. Intratesticular testosterone collapses even as blood levels look excellent, and spermatogenesis stops. Testosterone is, in effect, a male contraceptive. Men are routinely and wrongly prescribed it for infertility, which reliably makes matters worse.

sections.heading: Transport, Maturation and Ejaculation
sections.body:
A sperm cell leaving the seminiferous tubule is not yet capable of fertilising anything.
