It is immotile, its surface is unfinished, and it must undergo a maturation programme in the epididymis lasting roughly 10 to 14 days as it is slowly propelled along that 4 to 6 metre coiled tube. During transit, membrane proteins are added and remodelled, cholesterol content is adjusted, the disulphide bonds cross-linking the protamines in the nucleus and the proteins of the tail are further oxidised to stiffen and stabilise both, and the cell acquires progressive motility and the ability to bind the outer coat of an egg. Sperm from the head of the epididymis fertilise poorly; sperm from the tail fertilise well. The tail of the epididymis and the first part of the vas also serve as the storage reservoir, holding perhaps half of the extragonadal sperm reserve.

Ejaculation itself is a two-stage reflex under autonomic control, and each stage can fail independently. Emission is the sympathetic phase, mediated by nerves from spinal segments T10 to L2. Smooth muscle in the epididymal tail, vas deferens, seminal vesicles and prostate contracts, depositing sperm and accessory fluid into the posterior urethra. Critically, the internal urethral sphincter at the bladder neck closes at the same moment, and this closure is what forces the ejaculate forward rather than backward. Expulsion is the second phase, largely somatic and mediated through the pudendal nerve from S2 to S4, in which the bulbospongiosus and ischiocavernosus muscles contract rhythmically at intervals of roughly 0.8 seconds to propel semen out of the urethra.

Several failure modes follow directly. If the bladder neck does not close, semen takes the path of least resistance into the bladder, producing retrograde ejaculation: the man experiences orgasm but produces little or no ejaculate, and sperm are found in a post-ejaculatory urine sample. This occurs after bladder neck or prostate surgery, in diabetic autonomic neuropathy, in multiple sclerosis and spinal injury, and with alpha-blocker drugs such as tamsulosin used for prostate enlargement. If the sympathetic emission phase fails entirely, there is anejaculation, common after retroperitoneal lymph node dissection for testicular cancer, where the sympathetic chain is at risk, and after spinal cord injury.

Once deposited in the vagina, semen coagulates within a minute into a gel, then liquefies over 15 to 30 minutes under the action of prostate-specific antigen and other proteases. Sperm swim into cervical mucus, which around ovulation becomes thin, alkaline and arranged in channels that favour progressive swimmers and exclude abnormal ones. Only a few hundred to a few thousand of the tens of millions deposited reach the fallopian tube. During this journey sperm undergo capacitation, a final biochemical activation involving cholesterol loss from the membrane and calcium influx, without which the acrosome reaction and fertilisation cannot occur.

sections.heading: Semen Analysis and What the Numbers Mean
sections.body:
Semen analysis is the cornerstone investigation, and its results are more often misread than any other common laboratory test. The sample is produced by masturbation after 2 to 7 days of abstinence, collected complete into a sterile wide-mouthed container, kept near body temperature and delivered to the laboratory within one hour. Shorter abstinence lowers volume and count; longer abstinence raises count but worsens motility and DNA quality. Lubricants and ordinary condoms are spermicidal and must be avoided.

The World Health Organization's sixth edition reference values, published in 2021, are derived from the lower fifth percentile of men whose partners conceived within twelve months. The key thresholds are: semen volume 1.4 millilitres or more; sperm concentration 16 million per millilitre or more; total sperm number 39 million per ejaculate or more; total motility 42 per cent or more; progressive motility 30 per cent or more; vitality 54 per cent or more live; and normal forms 4 per cent or more by strict Kruger morphology criteria.

Those numbers are reference limits, not pass marks, and this distinction is the single most important thing to understand about the test. A man at the fourth percentile is not sterile; he simply sits in the region where the men who took longer to conceive are concentrated. Fertility is a continuum, and the parameters together predict outcome far better than any one alone. Equally, roughly 5 per cent of fertile men fall below at least one limit by definition. The 4 per cent morphology threshold routinely alarms patients who assume it means 96 per cent of their sperm are defective, when in fact strict criteria are deliberately punishing and 4 per cent is normal.

Biological variability is large. Repeat samples from the same man commonly differ by 30 per cent or more in concentration, so no clinical decision should rest on a single analysis. At least two samples taken several weeks apart, ideally more than 4 weeks apart to sample different production cycles, are standard.

The descriptive vocabulary is worth knowing: oligozoospermia means low concentration; asthenozoospermia, reduced motility; teratozoospermia, abnormal forms; the common combination is oligoasthenoteratozoospermia. Azoospermia means no sperm at all in the pellet after the sample is centrifuged, a finding that must be confirmed on a second, carefully centrifuged specimen before any conclusion is drawn. Aspermia means no ejaculate is produced at all.

Additional observations carry information. A low-volume, acidic, fructose-negative sample suggests obstruction of the ejaculatory ducts or absence of the vasa and seminal vesicles. Large numbers of white blood cells, above one million per millilitre, suggest infection or inflammation. Extensive clumping of sperm raises the possibility of antisperm antibodies. Failure of the sample to liquefy within an hour points to prostatic dysfunction, and a pH below 7.0 in a low-volume sample is a classic signature of absent or obstructed seminal vesicles, since the alkaline vesicle secretion is what normally raises semen pH to between 7.2 and 8.0.

sections.heading: Pre-testicular Causes: When the Signal Fails
sections.body:
Pre-testicular infertility means the testes are potentially capable but are not receiving the hormonal instructions they need. This group is comparatively uncommon, perhaps 2 to 5 per cent of male infertility, but it deserves attention out of proportion to its frequency because it is the most treatable category by a wide margin. A man with hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism who is correctly diagnosed can often father children with injections alone, no surgery and no laboratory fertilisation.

The blood picture is characteristic: low or inappropriately normal FSH and LH alongside low testosterone. The instruction is missing, so the testis is quiet, and testis volume is typically small and soft.

Congenital forms present at or after the expected age of puberty. Kallmann syndrome results from failure of the GnRH-secreting neurones to migrate from the olfactory placode into the hypothalamus during embryonic development, so affected men have both absent GnRH and, characteristically, an impaired or absent sense of smell, a combination that should always prompt hormonal testing. Several genes are implicated, including ANOS1 on the X chromosome, FGFR1, PROKR2 and CHD7. Normosmic isolated hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism is the same endocrine problem with a normal sense of smell.

Acquired causes are more common and often overlooked. A pituitary adenoma may compress the gonadotroph cells; prolactin-secreting adenomas do additional damage because high prolactin directly suppresses GnRH pulsatility. Any man with low testosterone and low gonadotrophins should have prolactin measured, and marked elevation warrants pituitary imaging, since a dopamine agonist such as cabergoline frequently restores both hormone levels and fertility without surgery. Infiltrative disease such as haemochromatosis, in which iron deposits in the pituitary and testis, sarcoidosis and tuberculosis, and damage from head injury, cranial radiotherapy or pituitary surgery all produce the same pattern.

Functional suppression is the largest group in practice and the most reversible. Severe systemic illness, uncontrolled diabetes, chronic kidney or liver disease, extreme exercise, and very low body weight all suppress the axis. So does marked obesity, through a distinct mechanism worth understanding: adipose tissue is rich in aromatase, which converts testosterone to oestradiol, and the resulting oestrogen excess feeds back to suppress LH and FSH while lowering testosterone further, a self-reinforcing loop. Weight loss reverses it.

Above all, exogenous androgens must be excluded by direct questioning. Anabolic steroid use for bodybuilding, and prescribed testosterone replacement given for fatigue or low libido, both shut down the axis and stop sperm production. This is now a leading identifiable cause of azoospermia in young men in some clinics. Recovery after stopping is usual but slow, commonly 4 to 12 months and occasionally longer than 2 years, and a minority never fully recover. Opioids, whether prescribed or illicit, suppress GnRH similarly, as do glucocorticoids in high dose.

sections.heading: Testicular Causes: When the Factory Fails
sections.body:
Testicular causes are by far the largest group, accounting for perhaps 65 to 80 per cent of identified male factor cases. Here the seminiferous tubules themselves are damaged, the hormonal signal is intact or amplified, and the characteristic blood picture is a raised FSH with reduced or absent inhibin B, reflecting a depleted germinal epithelium. Testis volume is usually reduced, and the difficulty of treatment is correspondingly greater, because a damaged germinal epithelium is not something medicine can currently regrow.

Varicocele is the most common identifiable abnormality, found in roughly 15 per cent of all men, 25 to 40 per cent of men with primary infertility and up to 80 per cent of those with secondary infertility. It is a dilation of the pampiniform venous plexus draining the testis, caused by incompetent valves and, on the left, by the anatomically awkward right-angled drainage of the left testicular vein into the left renal vein rather than directly into the vena cava. Roughly 85 to 90 per cent are left-sided or bilateral. The mechanism of damage is probably a combination of raised scrotal temperature from stagnant venous blood, defeating the countercurrent cooling arrangement, together with venous reflux of adrenal and renal metabolites and consequent oxidative stress. Clinically it is graded: grade 3 visible through the scrotal skin, grade 2 palpable at rest, grade 1 palpable only on Valsalva. The important honest caveat is that most men with varicocele are fertile, so its mere presence does not establish causation.

Cryptorchidism, failure of the testis to descend into the scrotum, damages the germinal epithelium because the undescended organ sits at body temperature. It affects about 3 per cent of full-term and up to 30 per cent of pre-term male infants, most descending spontaneously in the first months. Surgical correction is now recommended between 6 and 18 months precisely because histological damage is measurable by the second year. A history of unilateral cryptorchidism roughly doubles the risk of subfertility; bilateral cases carry a far higher risk, with paternity rates around 35 to 65 per cent. Cryptorchidism also raises testicular cancer risk several-fold, and that risk is not abolished by orchidopexy.

Other testicular insults include mumps orchitis after puberty, which affects perhaps 20 to 30 per cent of post-pubertal males with mumps and can cause irreversible atrophy; testicular torsion, where the blood supply is twisted off and salvage becomes unlikely beyond 6 to 8 hours; trauma; and testicular cancer, which impairs semen quality even before treatment begins. Cancer therapy is a major cause in its own right, with alkylating agents such as cyclophosphamide and procarbazine, and direct testicular radiation, being the most damaging. Sperm banking before any gonadotoxic treatment is essential and must be offered to every such patient.

sections.heading: Genetic and Chromosomal Causes
sections.body:
A genetic abnormality is identified in roughly 15 per cent of men with azoospermia and 5 per cent of those with severe oligozoospermia, and the proportion rises as sperm counts fall. Testing matters not only for diagnosis but because several of these conditions are transmissible to children conceived by assisted reproduction, which makes genetic counselling an ethical obligation rather than an optional extra.

Klinefelter syndrome, the 47,XXY karyotype, is the single most common genetic cause, present in about 1 in 600 male births and in 10 to 12 per cent of azoospermic men. The extra X chromosome causes progressive loss of germ cells, accelerating around puberty, so that by adulthood the testes are characteristically small and firm, typically under 4 millilitres, with raised FSH and LH and low testosterone. Many men are diagnosed only during a fertility evaluation. Encouragingly, microdissection testicular sperm extraction retrieves usable sperm in roughly 40 to 50 per cent of these men, and healthy chromosomally normal children have been born as a result, though earlier intervention appears to give better odds.

Y chromosome microdeletions occur in the azoospermia factor regions of the long arm, designated AZFa, AZFb and AZFc, and are found in about 5 to 10 per cent of men with azoospermia or severe oligozoospermia. The prognostic distinction is clinically decisive. Complete deletion of AZFa or AZFb predicts essentially zero chance of retrieving sperm surgically, and testing therefore spares the man a futile operation. Deletion of AZFc, the most common, is compatible with sperm retrieval in perhaps 50 to 75 per cent of cases and sometimes with a low natural sperm count. Any son conceived will inherit the deletion and the same infertility, which must be discussed frankly beforehand.

Mutations in the CFTR gene, the cystic fibrosis gene, cause congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens, responsible for 1 to 2 per cent of all male infertility and up to 25 per cent of obstructive azoospermia. These men produce sperm normally but have no conduit; the seminal vesicles are frequently absent too, giving the characteristic low-volume, acidic, fructose-negative ejaculate. Because their partner may be a carrier, she must be screened before treatment, since two carriers risk a child with classical cystic fibrosis.

Other causes include balanced chromosomal translocations and inversions, roughly ten times more common in infertile than fertile men, which impair meiotic pairing and raise the risk of miscarriage and unbalanced offspring; Kallmann syndrome and other hypogonadotrophic genetic disorders; androgen receptor mutations producing partial insensitivity; and the ciliary disorders such as primary ciliary dyskinesia, where the same dynein defect that impairs airway cilia leaves sperm tails immotile. Standard practice is to offer karyotype and Y microdeletion testing when concentration falls below 5 million per millilitre, and CFTR testing whenever the vasa are impalpable.

sections.heading: Post-testicular Causes: Obstruction and Delivery Failure
sections.body:
Post-testicular causes are the good news of male infertility. Sperm production is normal or near normal; the problem is purely plumbing or delivery. Because the germ cells are intact, these men can almost always become genetic fathers, either through reconstructive surgery or by retrieving sperm directly and using it in the laboratory. Obstruction accounts for roughly 40 per cent of azoospermia, and the clinical clue is the combination of azoospermia with normal FSH, normal inhibin B and normal testicular volume, since a working factory feeding a blocked pipe leaves the hormonal loop undisturbed.

Vasectomy is the most common cause worldwide, and it is deliberate. Reversal by vasovasostomy achieves return of sperm to the ejaculate in 70 to 95 per cent of cases and pregnancy in 30 to 75 per cent, with results depending overwhelmingly on the obstructive interval: outcomes are best within 3 years of the vasectomy and decline steadily thereafter, partly because prolonged back-pressure damages the epididymis and partly because antisperm antibodies develop. If the fluid found at the cut end of the vas contains no sperm, a secondary epididymal obstruction has usually developed and the more demanding vasoepididymostomy is required.

Congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens, tied to CFTR mutations, presents with impalpable vasa on examination, a finding any competent examiner can make in seconds and one that immediately explains a low-volume, acidic, fructose-negative azoospermic sample. It is not reconstructable; sperm are retrieved from the epididymis or testis instead.

Acquired obstruction follows infection, particularly gonorrhoea, chlamydia and tuberculosis affecting the epididymis, and follows surgery, notably childhood hernia repair, where the vas can be injured or ligated inadvertently. Ejaculatory duct obstruction, whether from a midline prostatic cyst, calculi or inflammation, produces the same low-volume acidic picture and can sometimes be relieved endoscopically by transurethral resection of the ejaculatory ducts.

Delivery failure is a separate group in which the tract is patent but semen does not emerge in the right direction or at all. Retrograde ejaculation is diagnosed by finding sperm in a post-ejaculatory urine sample and can often be treated medically with sympathomimetic drugs such as pseudoephedrine or imipramine taken before intercourse, which tighten the bladder neck; failing that, sperm are harvested from alkalinised urine. Anejaculation after spinal cord injury or retroperitoneal surgery may respond to penile vibratory stimulation or, if not, to rectal probe electroejaculation under anaesthesia.

Finally, immunological obstruction of function rather than of anatomy is caused by antisperm antibodies, which arise when the blood-testis barrier is breached by vasectomy, trauma, torsion or infection and the immune system meets sperm antigens it has never been tolerised to. Antibodies coating sperm impair motility and prevent penetration of cervical mucus. Sexual dysfunction, meaning erectile failure, severe premature ejaculation or simply intercourse that never occurs at the fertile time, is the last and most often unspoken member of this category.

sections.heading: Lifestyle, Heat, Environment and Oxidative Stress
sections.body:
Lifestyle factors rarely cause absolute sterility on their own, but they shift a man's monthly probability of conception downward, and in a couple already close to the margin that shift decides the outcome. They are also, uniquely among the causes, entirely under the couple's own control and cost nothing to address.

Heat is the most mechanistically direct. Spermatogenesis requires a testicular temperature of about 34 to 35 degrees Celsius, and experimental heating of the scrotum by as little as 1 to 2 degrees for several weeks measurably reduces sperm concentration. Practically, this implicates prolonged hot baths and saunas, laptop computers rested directly on the lap, which have been shown to raise scrotal temperature by more than 2 degrees within an hour, prolonged driving and sedentary occupations, and industrial heat exposure in foundries and bakeries. Tight underwear has a smaller effect than folklore suggests but is not zero. The reassuring corollary is that heat-related suppression is reversible, though the 3-month production cycle means improvement is not visible for at least that long.

Tobacco smoking reduces sperm concentration by roughly 15 to 20 per cent, motility by around 10 per cent and normal morphology similarly, and it substantially increases sperm DNA fragmentation. Cannabis interferes with the endocannabinoid signalling that sperm use in capacitation and is associated with lower counts and abnormal motility. Heavy alcohol intake, above about 14 to 20 standard units a week, lowers testosterone and worsens semen parameters; modest intake appears to have little effect. Anabolic steroid use, as noted, is catastrophic and frequently concealed by patients.

Obesity acts through several routes at once: aromatase in adipose tissue converts testosterone to oestradiol and suppresses the axis, the suprapubic fat pad insulates the scrotum and raises its temperature, and metabolic syndrome generates systemic oxidative stress. A body mass index above 30 is associated with roughly a 25 per cent reduction in sperm concentration and a measurable rise in DNA fragmentation.

Occupational and environmental exposures are real but often overstated in popular accounts. The clearly established agents include lead, cadmium, mercury, organic solvents such as glycol ethers, and certain pesticides, notably the nematocide dibromochloropropane, which caused mass sterility among production workers in the 1970s and remains the clearest single demonstration of chemical infertility in men. Endocrine-disrupting chemicals such as bisphenol A and phthalates show consistent associations in observational studies and clear effects in animals, but the size of the human effect at ordinary exposure levels is genuinely uncertain and should be described as such.

The common final pathway for many of these is oxidative stress. Reactive oxygen species are needed in small amounts for capacitation, but in excess they attack the polyunsaturated lipids of the sperm membrane and fragment its DNA, in a cell that has discarded almost all its antioxidant machinery.

sections.heading: Medications, Drugs and Iatrogenic Damage
sections.body:
A drug history is one of the highest-yield parts of a fertility consultation, because medication effects are common, frequently unrecognised and usually reversible on withdrawal. Prescribers rarely mention fertility, and patients rarely connect a tablet taken for something unrelated with a failure to conceive.

Exogenous testosterone in any form, gel, patch, injection or pellet, suppresses gonadotrophins and stops sperm production. It should be regarded as contraception in a man wanting children. Anabolic-androgenic steroids do the same more forcefully, often combined with human chorionic gonadotrophin and aromatase inhibitors in ways that complicate recovery. After stopping, semen parameters typically recover over 4 to 12 months, though a minority take longer than 2 years and a few never return to baseline.

Cytotoxic chemotherapy is the most damaging identifiable class. Alkylating agents, cyclophosphamide, chlorambucil, busulfan, melphalan and procarbazine, are the worst, and their effect is cumulative and dose-dependent: cyclophosphamide doses above roughly 7.5 grams per square metre carry a high risk of permanent azoospermia. Cisplatin-based regimens for testicular cancer cause temporary azoospermia in most men with recovery in perhaps 50 to 80 per cent by 5 years. Direct testicular radiation is severely toxic at very low doses, with transient azoospermia after 0.2 to 0.7 gray and permanent sterility likely above 2 to 6 gray. The clinical imperative is unambiguous: offer sperm cryopreservation to every post-pubertal male before any gonadotoxic therapy begins, even when time is short, since a single sample banked is better than none.

Among ordinary prescriptions, sulfasalazine, used for inflammatory bowel disease and rheumatoid arthritis, reversibly reduces sperm count and motility in the majority of men who take it, and switching to mesalazine typically restores parameters within 2 to 3 months. Finasteride and dutasteride, taken for hair loss and prostatic enlargement, lower semen volume and in some men reduce sperm counts markedly. Ketoconazole and spironolactone have antiandrogenic effects. Colchicine, methotrexate and mycophenolate have all been implicated. Alpha-blockers such as tamsulosin cause retrograde or absent ejaculation. Cimetidine acts as an androgen receptor antagonist.

Opioids deserve particular emphasis given the scale of their use: chronic opioid therapy suppresses GnRH release and produces hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism in a substantial fraction of long-term users, often unnoticed. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors delay ejaculation, reduce libido and have been associated with increased sperm DNA fragmentation. Some antipsychotics raise prolactin sharply and suppress the axis by that route.

The practical rule is that no medication should be stopped abruptly on fertility grounds alone. The right response is a conversation with the prescriber about whether an equally effective alternative exists, weighing the underlying condition against the delay. A man with severe ulcerative colitis is not helped by a relapse, and uncontrolled epilepsy or psychosis is a far greater threat to a future family than a temporarily reduced sperm count. Where a drug genuinely cannot be changed, sperm banking before or during treatment preserves the option regardless of what the medication does. Recovery timelines should also be stated realistically: because a full production cycle runs about 3 months, no repeat semen analysis after stopping a drug is meaningful before 3 months have passed, and 6 months gives a fairer picture.

sections.heading: The Clinical Evaluation, Step by Step
sections.body:
A male fertility evaluation is inexpensive, quick and highly informative when done in a disciplined order, and it should begin at the same time as the female partner's assessment rather than after it. The sequence below reflects standard urological practice.

The history establishes duration of attempted conception, coital frequency and timing, and whether either partner has conceived before, since previous paternity narrows the field considerably. It then covers childhood events, particularly undescended testes, hernia repair, torsion and mumps after puberty; past infections including sexually transmitted infection, epididymitis and tuberculosis; surgery on the groin, scrotum, bladder, prostate or retroperitoneum; systemic disease, especially diabetes, kidney and liver disease and past cancer treatment; every medication and supplement including anything bought online; alcohol, tobacco, cannabis and anabolic steroids, asked directly and without judgement; occupational heat, solvent, pesticide and metal exposure; and sexual function, including erection, ejaculation and libido. Anosmia points to Kallmann syndrome and should always be asked about.

The examination takes 3 minutes and answers questions no blood test can. Testis volume is measured with an orchidometer, with anything under 15 millilitres suggesting reduced spermatogenic tissue and under 5 millilitres suggesting primary failure. Consistency matters: small and firm suggests Klinefelter, small and soft suggests hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism or post-pubertal damage. Both vasa are palpated along the cord, since impalpable vasa diagnose congenital absence immediately. The epididymis is assessed for fullness or induration suggesting obstruction. The cord is examined standing, with and without Valsalva, for varicocele. Secondary sexual characteristics, body habitus, gynaecomastia and the position of the urethral meatus are noted.
steps: Obtain two semen analyses at least four weeks apart, each after two to seven days of abstinence, before drawing any conclusion; single-sample variation of thirty per cent or more is normal.
If any parameter is abnormal, or if there is a suggestive history, measure morning total testosterone and FSH; add LH, prolactin and oestradiol if testosterone is low.

Interpret the pattern rather than the individual values: high FSH with low testis volume indicates primary testicular failure; low FSH and LH with low testosterone indicates a pituitary or hypothalamic cause; normal FSH with azoospermia and normal testis volume indicates obstruction.

Perform scrotal ultrasound with Doppler if the examination is difficult, if a mass is suspected, or to confirm and grade a varicocele; every infertile man should have testicular cancer excluded, since the risk is raised several-fold.
Perform transrectal ultrasound where the ejaculate volume is under 1.4 millilitres with acidic pH, looking for ejaculatory duct obstruction, midline cysts or absent seminal vesicles.
Send a post-ejaculatory urine specimen whenever ejaculate volume is very low or absent and the vasa are present, to detect retrograde ejaculation.

Request karyotype and Y chromosome microdeletion testing when sperm concentration is below five million per millilitre or in any azoospermia, and CFTR mutation analysis when either vas is impalpable, screening the female partner for CFTR carriage before treatment.

Consider sperm DNA fragmentation testing in recurrent pregnancy loss, repeated failure of assisted reproduction, or unexplained infertility with normal conventional parameters, recognising that its role remains debated.

sections.heading: Treatment: Medical and Surgical
sections.body:
Treatment divides cleanly into three ambitions: correct a specific reversible cause, improve semen quality empirically, or bypass the problem with assisted reproduction. The first is always preferable when available, because it restores the possibility of natural conception in future pregnancies too.

Specific medical treatment works best in hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism, where the results are among the most satisfying in medicine. Human chorionic gonadotrophin, which mimics LH, is given by injection typically at 1,500 to 2,500 international units two or three times a week to restart intratesticular testosterone. If sperm do not appear after 4 to 6 months, FSH activity is added as recombinant FSH or human menopausal gonadotrophin, usually 75 to 150 units three times weekly. Spermatogenesis returns in 70 to 90 per cent of men, but slowly: expect 6 to 24 months, and counsel patients accordingly. Hyperprolactinaemia is treated with cabergoline, typically 0.25 to 0.5 milligrams twice weekly, which normalises prolactin in most cases and often restores fertility without further intervention.

Empirical medical therapy for idiopathic oligozoospermia has a weaker evidence base and should be described honestly as such. Clomiphene citrate, 25 to 50 milligrams daily or on alternate days, blocks oestrogen feedback at the hypothalamus and raises endogenous LH, FSH and testosterone; anastrozole, an aromatase inhibitor at 1 milligram daily, is used where the testosterone to oestradiol ratio is low, which is common in obese men. Both raise hormone levels reliably; whether they raise live birth rates is not established by good randomised evidence. Antioxidant supplementation with vitamins C and E, zinc, selenium, coenzyme Q10, L-carnitine and folate is widely used and biologically plausible given sperm vulnerability to oxidative damage, but the trials are small and heterogeneous and a large well-conducted study found no benefit in live birth. Antibiotics are appropriate for demonstrated genital tract infection and not otherwise.

Surgical treatment has clearer indications. Varicocelectomy is offered to men with a palpable varicocele, abnormal semen parameters and an otherwise fertile partner; the microsurgical subinguinal approach has the lowest recurrence rate, roughly 1 per cent, and the fewest complications. Semen parameters improve in perhaps 60 to 70 per cent, with typical gains of around 10 million per millilitre in concentration and 10 percentage points in motility, and natural pregnancy rates rise by a modest but real margin. Repair of a subclinical varicocele detected only on ultrasound is not supported.

Vasectomy reversal and vasoepididymostomy reconstruct obstruction. Transurethral resection of the ejaculatory ducts relieves distal obstruction in selected men. Where the cause is retrograde ejaculation, sympathomimetics come first and sperm harvest from alkalinised urine second.

Two general principles govern the whole of treatment. The first is that the female partner's age sets the clock: a treatment taking 18 months is reasonable when she is 28 and often unreasonable when she is 40, and couples should be told this arithmetic explicitly. The second is that no treatment can be judged before a full spermatogenic cycle has elapsed, so semen should not be reassessed sooner than 3 months afterwards, and 6 months is fairer for varicocelectomy, whose benefit accrues for up to a year.

sections.heading: Assisted Reproduction and Surgical Sperm Retrieval
sections.body:
When the cause cannot be corrected, assisted reproduction bypasses it, and the choice of technique is dictated almost entirely by how many motile sperm can be assembled.

Intrauterine insemination is the least invasive option. The ejaculate is washed to remove seminal plasma, which would otherwise cause painful uterine cramping, and concentrated, then placed directly into the uterine cavity through a fine catheter around the time of ovulation, often with mild ovarian stimulation of the female partner. It bypasses the cervix and shortens the journey. It requires a total motile sperm count after preparation of at least about 5 million, with better results above 10 million, and at least one patent fallopian tube. Success is modest, roughly 8 to 15 per cent live birth per cycle, and three to six cycles are usually attempted before moving on.

Conventional in vitro fertilisation places roughly 50,000 to 100,000 motile sperm in a dish with each retrieved egg and lets fertilisation happen unaided. It needs reasonable numbers and function, and in severe male factor it risks total fertilisation failure.

Intracytoplasmic sperm injection, ICSI, introduced by Palermo and colleagues in Brussels in 1992, transformed the field. A single sperm is immobilised, drawn into a glass micropipette a few micrometres across and injected directly through the egg's outer coat and membrane into its cytoplasm. Every barrier the sperm would normally have to overcome, motility, cervical mucus, the zona pellucida, membrane fusion, is bypassed. One viable sperm per egg suffices, so ICSI works for counts that would once have meant certain childlessness. Fertilisation rates are typically 70 to 80 per cent per injected egg, and live birth rates track the female partner's age far more than the sperm's quality, from roughly 35 to 40 per cent per embryo transfer under 35 down to under 10 per cent over 42.

Where no sperm reach the ejaculate, they are retrieved surgically. In obstructive azoospermia, sperm are abundant upstream and simple aspiration from the epididymis or a testicular biopsy succeeds in essentially 100 per cent of cases. In non-obstructive azoospermia, where production itself is failing, sperm may exist only in scattered pockets of surviving tubules; microdissection testicular sperm extraction, in which the testis is opened under an operating microscope at 15 to 25 times magnification and plumper, more opaque tubules are selectively sampled, retrieves sperm in roughly 40 to 60 per cent overall, better than blind biopsy and with less tissue removed.

The honest caveats matter. ICSI children have a modestly increased rate of congenital anomalies, in the region of a 30 to 40 per cent relative increase on a low baseline, and increased rates of sex chromosome abnormalities and imprinting disorders, though how much is the technique and how much the underlying infertility remains genuinely unresolved.

sections.heading: Prognosis, Unexplained Cases and What to Do When Nothing Works
sections.body:
Between 30 and 50 per cent of men with abnormal semen parameters receive no explanation at all, a category labelled idiopathic male infertility. This is an admission of ignorance rather than a diagnosis, and it should be presented that way. Some of these cases will eventually be explained by genetic variants not yet catalogued, by subtle epigenetic changes in sperm, by DNA fragmentation that conventional analysis cannot see, or by exposures nobody thought to ask about. Saying plainly that the cause is unknown is more useful, and more honest, than inventing one.

Prognosis in subfertility is better than couples usually fear. Because most men are subfertile rather than sterile, spontaneous pregnancy continues to occur during investigation and while waiting for treatment, at rates of perhaps 20 to 25 per cent over 2 years even with clearly abnormal parameters. The strongest predictors of a natural conception are total motile sperm count, the duration of infertility so far, and above all the female partner's age. Age is the ruthless variable: a woman of 30 has time to attempt several approaches in sequence, while a woman of 39 does not, and the correct advice for an identical male problem can therefore be entirely different for the two couples.

Failure modes in the process itself are worth naming. The commonest is a decision made on one semen analysis; the second is a man given testosterone for low libido or fatigue while trying to conceive, which stops production; the third is an infertile man never examined, so that impalpable vasa, a large varicocele or a testicular tumour goes unfound; the fourth is proceeding to invasive treatment of the female partner without any male evaluation at all. Each is avoidable.

When treatment fails, or when the diagnosis makes success impossible, the remaining paths are real ones and should be laid out without euphemism. Donor sperm insemination achieves cumulative pregnancy rates comparable to those of fertile couples and is far cheaper than repeated ICSI cycles. Adoption and fostering are not consolation prizes. Choosing to remain without children is a legitimate outcome that some couples reach deliberately and with relief once the treadmill stops.

The psychological weight of male infertility is consistently underestimated by clinicians. Studies find levels of distress in infertile men comparable to those in people diagnosed with cancer or serious cardiac disease, and men are markedly less likely than their partners to seek or accept support. Diagnosis frequently arrives with an unspoken conflation of fertility and masculinity that nothing in the biology justifies. Naming this explicitly, offering counselling as routine rather than as a sign of fragility, and setting an agreed limit in advance on how many cycles or how many years the couple will attempt, are among the most valuable interventions available, and none of them requires a laboratory.

guides.safetyNote: Never start or stop a prescribed medication on fertility grounds without speaking to the prescriber. Testosterone in any form suppresses sperm production and must not be taken by a man trying to conceive. A new painless testicular lump, a sudden severely painful testis (possible torsion, where salvage is unlikely beyond six to eight hours), or breast growth with low testosterone all need urgent medical assessment rather than a fertility work-up. Anyone facing chemotherapy, testicular radiotherapy or gonadal surgery should be offered sperm banking before treatment begins. This guide explains the biology and the options; it does not replace assessment by a doctor, and both partners should be investigated together.

guides.title: Prostate Health and Screening
guides.summary: How the prostate works, the three diseases that affect it — benign enlargement, prostatitis, and cancer — and an honest, evidence-based walk through PSA screening, diagnosis, grading, and treatment choices.

sections.heading: Why the Prostate Deserves Attention
sections.body: The prostate is a small gland, roughly the size and shape of a walnut and weighing 20 to 30 grams in a healthy young adult, that sits directly beneath the bladder and completely surrounds the urethra, the tube that carries urine out of the body. That location explains nearly everything that follows in this guide. A gland wrapped around the urinary outflow tract can, when it enlarges, becomes inflamed, or turns cancerous, squeeze that tract and change how a man urinates — which is why prostate disease so often announces itself in the bathroom rather than with pain. Only males have a prostate; its job is to produce a portion of the fluid that carries sperm. Three conditions account for nearly all prostate trouble. Benign prostatic hyperplasia, usually shortened to BPH, is a non-cancerous enlargement that affects about half of men by age 60 and up to 90 percent of men in their eighties. Prostatitis, an inflammation that sometimes involves bacteria and often does not, is the most common urologic diagnosis in men under 50. Prostate cancer is the most commonly diagnosed internal cancer in men in most of the world: roughly one man in eight will be diagnosed during his lifetime, yet only about one in 40 to one in 50 dies of it in countries with modern care. That wide gap between how common the cancer is and how often it kills is the central tension in prostate medicine. Many prostate cancers grow so slowly that a man dies of something else decades later, never knowing he had it; a minority are aggressive killers that spread to bone and resist treatment. Screening — chiefly the PSA blood test — can find cancers early enough to cure, but it also finds harmless ones, and treating harmless cancers causes real damage: incontinence, impotence, anxiety, and cost. Reasonable experts have disagreed for thirty years about where the balance lies, and the honest position, reflected in every major guideline today, is that screening is a personal decision to be made with information rather than a simple yes or no. This guide gives you that information. It begins with the anatomy and hormonal machinery of the gland, because the mechanisms explain both the diseases and the treatments. It then works through BPH and prostatitis, which are far more common than cancer and frequently confused with it. The second half covers cancer itself: who is at risk, exactly what the PSA test measures and what corrupts it, what the major screening trials actually showed, how a suspicious result becomes a diagnosis through MRI and biopsy, how pathologists grade aggressiveness, and what the treatment paths — including the increasingly common choice to monitor rather than treat — realistically involve. A man who reads it should be able to sit across from a clinician, or reason alone far from one, and make decisions about his own gland with clear eyes.

sections.heading: Anatomy: A Gland Built Around a Tube
sections.body: Understanding prostate disease starts with a mental map of the gland. Picture the bladder as a reservoir at the bottom of the abdomen. Emerging from its floor is the urethra, and for the first three centimeters or so of its journey the urethra passes directly through the middle of the prostate — this segment is called the prostatic urethra. The gland sits just in front of the rectum, separated from it by only a few millimeters of tissue, which is why a clinician's gloved finger in the rectum can feel the back surface of the prostate directly; this is the digital rectal examination. Below the prostate lies the external urinary sphincter, the muscle a man consciously squeezes to hold urine, and running along the gland's back corners are the neurovascular bundles, paired cords of nerves and vessels that carry the signals responsible for erection. Their nearness explains why prostate surgery and radiation so often affect continence and sexual function. The pathologist John McNeal showed in the 1960s and 1970s that the prostate is not uniform but organized into zones, and the zones behave very differently. The peripheral zone forms the back and sides — roughly 70 percent of the glandular tissue — and it is where about 70 to 80 percent of cancers arise; conveniently, it is also the part a rectal examination can reach. The transition zone is a small cuff of tissue immediately surrounding the urethra; it is the exclusive birthplace of BPH, which is why benign enlargement squeezes the urethra so effectively, and it hosts perhaps 10 to 20 percent of cancers, often ones found incidentally when tissue is removed to relieve blockage. The central zone surrounds the ejaculatory ducts — the channels through which sperm from the testicles, having been stored in the seminal vesicles behind the bladder, passes into the urethra during ejaculation — and it gives rise to only a small percentage of cancers. A fibromuscular band forms the gland's front surface and contains little glandular tissue at all. The whole organ is wrapped in a thin capsule; whether a cancer is confined within that capsule or has broken through it is one of the most important facts in staging. Two practical consequences fall straight out of this anatomy. First, because most cancers begin in the peripheral zone, far from the urethra, early prostate cancer usually causes no urinary symptoms whatsoever — a man can harbor a dangerous tumor and feel completely normal, which is the entire argument for screening blood tests rather than waiting for symptoms. Second, because BPH begins in the transition zone hugging the urethra, benign disease causes urinary symptoms early and loudly. The common assumption that trouble urinating signals cancer therefore has the logic almost exactly backwards: obstructive symptoms usually point to the benign disease, while the cancer is typically silent until it is advanced enough to invade the urethra, the bladder neck, or the bones of the spine and pelvis.

sections.heading: The Hormonal Engine: Testosterone, DHT, and Growth
sections.body: The prostate is an androgen-dependent organ: it is built, maintained, and — when diseased — driven by male hormones. Testosterone, made mainly in the testicles under the direction of pituitary signals, circulates in the blood and diffuses into prostate cells. Inside the gland, an enzyme called 5-alpha-reductase, particularly its type 2 form which is concentrated in prostate tissue, converts testosterone into dihydrotestosterone, or DHT. DHT is the true working hormone of the prostate: it binds the androgen receptor several-fold more tightly than testosterone itself and holds on longer, switching on the genes that tell prostate cells to grow, survive, and secrete. The proof of how essential this pathway is comes from rare natural experiments. Men born with a genetic deficiency of 5-alpha-reductase type 2 develop only a vestigial prostate and, as far as medicine has observed, essentially never develop BPH or prostate cancer. Men castrated before puberty likewise never develop either disease. These observations are the foundation of two major drug classes. The 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors finasteride and dutasteride block the conversion step, shrink benign glands by roughly a quarter, and — important for anyone interpreting laboratory results — cut the blood PSA level approximately in half within six to twelve months, so a measured PSA in a man taking these drugs must be mentally doubled to be compared against normal ranges. At the other end of the severity spectrum, androgen deprivation therapy for advanced cancer removes the hormonal fuel supply altogether, either surgically or with injections that shut down testicular production; the American physician Charles Huggins showed in 1941 that metastatic prostate cancer regresses dramatically when deprived of androgens, a discovery that earned the 1966 Nobel Prize and still anchors treatment of advanced disease today. Hormones also explain the gland's secretions. Prostatic fluid contributes roughly a quarter of the volume of semen, with most of the remainder coming from the seminal vesicles. The prostate's contribution is chemically distinctive: it is loaded with citrate, with zinc at the highest concentration found in any soft tissue of the body, and with enzymes — most famously prostate-specific antigen. PSA is not a mysterious cancer chemical; it is a protease, a protein-cutting enzyme also called human kallikrein 3, whose everyday job is to liquefy the gel-like clot that semen forms after ejaculation so that sperm can swim free. Healthy cells make it constantly and secrete it into the ducts of the gland, where it belongs. Only a tiny fraction normally leaks backward into the bloodstream. Anything that disrupts the architecture separating gland ducts from blood vessels — cancer, inflammation, infection, physical pressure, or simply the disordered growth of BPH — lets more PSA escape into circulation. That single fact, that PSA in blood is a signal of disturbed prostate tissue of any kind rather than of cancer specifically, is the key to every strength and every weakness of PSA screening.

sections.heading: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: How the Gland Chokes Its Own Plumbing
sections.body: Benign prostatic hyperplasia is exactly what its name says: an increase in the number of cells — hyperplasia — that is not cancer and does not become cancer. Beginning typically in a man's forties, nodules of new glandular and muscular tissue form in the transition zone, the cuff of prostate immediately surrounding the urethra. Why this happens is only partly understood; the process requires DHT and aging, and probably involves a shifting balance between androgens and estrogens along with chronic low-grade inflammation, but no single cause has been proven. What is thoroughly understood is the mechanics of the obstruction, which has two distinct components, and the distinction matters because different drugs attack each one. The static component is simple bulk: the enlarged transition zone physically narrows the urethral channel, like a fist slowly closing around a straw. A normal prostate of 20 to 30 grams can grow to 50, 80, or beyond 100 grams. The dynamic component is muscular tone: the prostate and bladder neck are rich in smooth muscle studded with alpha-1 adrenergic receptors, and when the sympathetic nervous system tightens that muscle — with stress, cold, or certain decongestant drugs — the channel narrows further without any change in gland size. This is why a man with BPH may urinate acceptably one day and barely at all another, and why cold-remedy decongestants such as pseudoephedrine can tip a borderline gland into complete blockage. Upstream, the bladder fights back. Forced to push urine through a resistant channel, its muscular wall — the detrusor — thickens and becomes irritable and overactive, which produces its own symptom family: sudden urgency, frequent urination, and waking repeatedly at night. Clinicians therefore divide lower urinary tract symptoms into voiding symptoms caused by the blockage itself — a weak or interrupted stream, hesitancy before flow starts, straining, dribbling at the end, a sense of incomplete emptying — and storage symptoms caused by the irritated bladder: frequency, urgency, and nocturia. In late, neglected disease the bladder decompensates: it stretches, loses contractile power, and retains a growing pool of residual urine. Stagnant urine breeds infection and bladder stones; back-pressure can transmit up the ureters and injure the kidneys; and the end stage is acute urinary retention, the abrupt and extremely painful inability to urinate at all, which is a genuine emergency requiring a catheter. Two clarifications save much worry. First, gland size correlates only loosely with symptoms — some men with huge prostates urinate well because the growth happens to bulge outward, while others with modestly enlarged glands are miserable because a small nodule sits exactly at the bladder neck. Second, BPH does not cause prostate cancer and having it does not raise cancer risk, but the two commonly coexist in the same aging gland, and BPH raises PSA, which is one of the chief reasons PSA screening produces so many false alarms.

sections.heading: Managing BPH: From Watchful Waiting to Surgery
sections.body: Because BPH is benign, treatment is driven entirely by how much the symptoms bother the man, balanced against the risks of intervention — with one exception: signs of harm such as retention, recurrent infections, bladder stones, blood in the urine, or kidney back-pressure push toward definitive treatment regardless of bother. Evaluation starts with a symptom questionnaire, most often the International Prostate Symptom Score, seven questions each scored 0 to 5 for a total of 0 to 35; scores under 8 are mild, 8 to 19 moderate, 20 and above severe. A urine test excludes infection and blood, a PSA is usually drawn, and an ultrasound may measure gland size and how much urine remains after voiding. For mild symptoms, lifestyle measures genuinely help: reducing evening fluids, moderating caffeine and alcohol (both are diuretics and bladder irritants), avoiding decongestants and antihistamines that tighten or weaken the outflow machinery, treating constipation, and double-voiding — urinating, waiting a moment, and trying again. Drug therapy has two main pillars matching the two components of obstruction. Alpha-blockers such as tamsulosin, alfuzosin, silodosin, and doxazosin relax the smooth muscle of the prostate and bladder neck within days, typically improving symptom scores promptly; their costs are dizziness from lowered blood pressure, retrograde ejaculation — semen slipping backward into the bladder, harmless but disconcerting — and, notably, floppy iris syndrome during cataract surgery, so any man on these drugs must tell his eye surgeon. The 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors finasteride and dutasteride starve the gland of DHT and shrink it by roughly 25 percent, but they need six to twelve months to work and only make sense for genuinely enlarged glands, roughly above 30 to 40 grams; a few percent of users report reduced libido or erectile difficulty, and the drugs halve measured PSA. The large MTOPS trial showed the two classes together reduce long-term progression — symptom worsening, retention, or need for surgery — by about two-thirds compared with placebo, substantially better than either alone in men with bigger glands. Daily tadalafil, a phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor, is an option that helps both urinary symptoms and erections. The herbal remedy saw palmetto, despite enormous popularity, performed no better than placebo in rigorous trials even at triple doses. When drugs fail or complications arrive, surgery relieves obstruction by removing or displacing transition-zone tissue. The reference operation remains transurethral resection of the prostate — TURP — in which tissue is shaved from inside the channel through a scope; it improves flow dramatically and durably, at the cost of retrograde ejaculation in most men, a small risk of incontinence or stricture, and a recovery involving days of catheterization. Laser enucleation handles even very large glands; simple prostatectomy removes the inner gland surgically for the largest. Newer minimally invasive options — UroLift implants that pin the lobes open, water-vapor ablation, prostatic artery embolization — trade somewhat less durable relief for preserved ejaculation and quicker recovery, a trade many younger men accept knowingly.

sections.heading: Prostatitis: Infection, Inflammation, and Pelvic Pain
sections.body: Prostatitis is really four different conditions sharing a name, and confusing them leads to years of mistreatment, so the National Institutes of Health classification is worth learning. Category I, acute bacterial prostatitis, is a true infection and a genuine emergency-adjacent illness. Bacteria — most often Escherichia coli and related gut organisms — ascend the urethra or seed the gland from infected urine, and the man becomes abruptly, systemically ill: high fever, chills, deep pelvic or low-back ache, burning urination, sometimes inability to urinate at all as the swollen gland clamps the urethra. The prostate is exquisitely tender on examination, and vigorous massage of it is avoided for fear of pushing bacteria into the bloodstream. Treatment is prompt antibiotics — intravenously if the man is very ill — continued for two to four weeks and often longer, because the inflamed gland is hard for drugs to penetrate; retention may require a catheter, and an abscess occasionally needs drainage. Treated properly, most men recover fully. Category II, chronic bacterial prostatitis, is subtler: the same organisms smolder in the gland for months, causing repeated urinary tract infections with the identical bacterium each time, low-grade pelvic discomfort, and painful ejaculation, with well periods in between. Diagnosis rests on localizing bacteria to prostatic fluid, and cure requires long antibiotic courses — four to six weeks or more of an agent that penetrates prostate tissue, classically a fluoroquinolone or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole — with relapse common enough that patience matters. Category III, chronic prostatitis/chronic pelvic pain syndrome, accounts for more than 90 percent of all prostatitis diagnoses and is the one most men with the label actually have. It is defined by at least three months of pelvic, perineal, penile, testicular, or ejaculatory pain and variable urinary symptoms with no demonstrable infection. Its cause is genuinely uncertain and probably varies from man to man: candidate mechanisms include a previous infection that left neurogenic inflammation behind, pelvic floor muscle tension and spasm, nerve sensitization in which the spinal cord amplifies normal signals into pain, urine refluxing into prostate ducts, and stress physiology — and honest clinicians say so rather than promising a quick fix. Because no single cause exists, no single treatment works; care that helps is multimodal, matching therapy to each man's pattern: an alpha-blocker if voiding symptoms dominate, pelvic floor physical therapy — often the most effective single intervention — when examination finds tight, tender pelvic muscles, anti-inflammatories for flares, heat, regular ejaculation, avoiding prolonged cycling pressure, and treating the anxiety and catastrophizing that chronic pain breeds. Repeated long antibiotic courses without evidence of bacteria help no one and select resistant organisms. Category IV is asymptomatic inflammation discovered incidentally in biopsies and needs no treatment at all. Two connections worth remembering: any prostatitis can raise PSA dramatically — sometimes into ranges that mimic cancer — and a PSA drawn during or soon after an episode should be repeated weeks later before any biopsy decision is made.

sections.heading: Prostate Cancer: A Common Cancer With an Uncommon Personality
sections.body: Nearly all prostate cancers — over 95 percent — are adenocarcinomas, meaning they arise from the gland-forming cells that line the prostate's ducts, and most begin in the peripheral zone at the back of the gland, far from the urethra. This geography is why early prostate cancer is almost always silent: nothing presses on the urinary channel until the disease is advanced. The biology that follows is unusual among major cancers in two ways. First, prostate cancer is extraordinarily common at the microscopic level. Autopsy studies of men who died of other causes find small hidden cancers in roughly a third of men over 50 and in well over half of men in their eighties — the finding behind the aphorism that many more men die with prostate cancer than of it. Second, the disease's pace spans an enormous range. Low-grade tumors can have volume doubling times measured in years and may never leave the gland in a man's remaining lifetime, while high-grade tumors invade, escape the capsule, and seed distant sites within a few years. Molecularly, the disease is driven above all by the androgen receptor: prostate cancer cells remain addicted to androgen signaling even after they escape the gland, which is why hormonal therapy works and why resistance eventually evolves through receptor amplification and mutation. About half of cancers in men of European descent carry a characteristic gene fusion called TMPRSS2-ERG, in which an androgen-controlled switch is welded to a growth-promoting gene, so the tumor's own fuel supply drives its accelerator; loss of tumor suppressors such as PTEN and, in aggressive disease, defects in DNA-repair genes like BRCA2 mark the more dangerous branches of the family tree. Prostate cancer is also typically multifocal — several separate tumors of different grades often coexist in one gland — which complicates any strategy aimed at treating only part of the prostate. When the disease spreads, it follows a signature route: first to lymph nodes in the pelvis, then overwhelmingly to bone, favoring the spine, pelvis, and ribs. Unlike most cancers, which dissolve bone, prostate metastases are usually osteoblastic — they provoke chaotic new bone formation — producing dense spots on scans, bone pain, fractures, and, when vertebrae are involved, the emergency of spinal cord compression. Advanced disease can also crowd out bone marrow, causing anemia and fatigue. Symptoms, when they finally come, therefore divide into two families: local ones — blood in urine or semen, new erectile failure, obstructive urination from a tumor reaching the urethra or bladder neck — and distant ones, chiefly persistent bone pain, most classically in the lower back at night, weight loss, and fatigue. Any of these in a man over 50 deserves evaluation, but the overriding practical point runs the other way: because the curable stage is the silent stage, waiting for symptoms is a strategy that mostly finds incurable disease, and that fact is the entire case for the screening discussion that follows.

sections.heading: Who Is at Risk: Age, Ancestry, and Inheritance
sections.body: Three risk factors for prostate cancer tower over all others: age, family history, and ancestry. Age is the strongest. The disease is rare before 40, uncommon before 50, and then climbs steeply; the median age at diagnosis in screened populations is in the mid-sixties, and the microscopic cancers found at autopsy accumulate decade by decade. Family history matters in a graded way. A single first-degree relative — father or brother — with prostate cancer roughly doubles a man's risk; two or more affected relatives multiply it further, toward three- or four-fold; and risk rises more when relatives were diagnosed young, before 55 or 60, which suggests inherited biology rather than the shared coincidence of two common late-life diagnoses. On top of family patterns sit specific inherited genes. Mutations in BRCA2 — the same gene famous for breast and ovarian cancer — raise prostate cancer risk several-fold and, more importantly, are associated with earlier, more aggressive, more lethal disease; BRCA1, ATM, CHEK2, and the Lynch-syndrome mismatch-repair genes carry smaller or less certain effects; and a recurrent mutation in HOXB13 is a rare but well-documented cause of hereditary prostate cancer. This is why modern guidelines treat men with BRCA2 mutations, and men whose family trees are heavy with prostate, breast, ovarian, or pancreatic cancer, as a distinct high-risk group deserving earlier and more deliberate screening — and why a man diagnosed with metastatic prostate cancer is now routinely offered germline genetic testing, since the answer changes both his treatment options and his relatives' screening. Ancestry is the third pillar. Men of African descent have roughly 1.7 times the incidence of prostate cancer compared with men of European descent and about twice the death rate; they are diagnosed younger and with more advanced disease on average. How much of this reflects inherited genetic variation — several risk variants are more common in African-ancestry populations — versus unequal access to screening and treatment is genuinely unsettled; the honest reading is that both contribute, and the practical consequence is uncontroversial: earlier screening conversations, typically starting at 40 to 45. Asian men living in Asia have historically low rates that rise within a generation or two of migration to Western countries, a classic signal that environment and diet matter, though pinning down which components has proven frustrating. Beyond these, the evidence thins. Obesity is associated less with getting prostate cancer than with getting aggressive prostate cancer and dying of it. Smoking worsens prostate cancer mortality. Diets heavy in processed meat and dairy show weak positive associations; lycopene-rich tomatoes and cruciferous vegetables show weak protective ones — none strong enough to build a prevention strategy on. Two large prevention trials taught hard lessons: finasteride cut overall cancer incidence by about a quarter in the PCPT trial but mostly by preventing low-grade disease, and the SELECT trial found that vitamin E supplements, far from protecting, increased prostate cancer risk by about 17 percent — a standing caution against assuming supplements are harmless. Vasectomy, despite decades of worry, shows no convincing causal link.

sections.heading: The PSA Test: What It Measures and What Corrupts It
sections.body: The prostate-specific antigen test measures the blood concentration, in nanograms per milliliter, of the semen-liquefying enzyme that healthy prostate cells make constantly. The name is precise: PSA is specific to the prostate, not to cancer. Any process that disturbs the gland's architecture lets more of it leak into the bloodstream, and interpreting the number is largely the art of separating those causes. Cancer raises PSA because malignant tissue is disorganized and leaky — per gram, cancer releases far more PSA into blood than benign tissue does. But BPH raises it too, simply by multiplying the amount of PSA-producing tissue; prostatitis and urinary infection can spike it dramatically, sometimes above 20 or 50 ng/mL, into ranges that mimic advanced cancer; urinary retention and catheterization raise it; a prostate biopsy raises it for weeks. Ejaculation can lift it modestly for up to 48 to 72 hours, which is why abstinence for two or three days before the draw is often advised; long bicycle rides may nudge it; a gentle rectal examination changes it little. In the other direction, finasteride and dutasteride cut it roughly in half, and obesity dilutes it modestly in a larger blood volume. Because PSA's half-life in blood is two to three days, a spike takes weeks to fully clear — so the single most useful rule in all of PSA interpretation is: never act on one elevated value. Repeat it after several weeks, untreated or after addressing any obvious cause, before doing anything else; a substantial fraction of elevations simply vanish. The traditional threshold of 4.0 ng/mL is a historical convenience, not a biological boundary. The Prostate Cancer Prevention Trial biopsied men with supposedly normal values and found cancer in about 15 percent of men with PSA below 4 — a small fraction of it high-grade — while among men with PSA between 4 and 10, only about one in four has cancer on biopsy. There is no PSA level with zero risk and no level that guarantees cancer; the number shifts probabilities. Several refinements sharpen it. Free PSA exploits the fact that PSA from cancer tends to circulate bound to proteins: when less than about 10 percent of total PSA is free, cancer probability is high, while above about 25 percent it is low. PSA density divides the level by gland volume measured on imaging, correcting for BPH; values above roughly 0.15 ng/mL per cubic centimeter raise suspicion. PSA velocity — the rate of rise per year — is intuitive but proved disappointing in formal testing and now carries little weight on its own. Age-specific ranges acknowledge that an older gland is a bigger gland. Newer blood and urine panels — the Prostate Health Index, the 4Kscore, urinary PCA3 and similar — combine markers to estimate specifically the risk of aggressive cancer, and are used mainly to decide whether a man with a modestly elevated PSA truly needs a biopsy. One more finding deserves respect: a PSA above 10, confirmed on repeat, carries a cancer probability around 50 percent or higher and warrants urologic referral rather than watchful drift.

sections.heading: The Screening Controversy: What the Trials Actually Showed
sections.body: Whether routine PSA screening saves enough lives to justify its harms is one of the most carefully studied and most contested questions in preventive medicine, and understanding the two landmark trials explains why thoughtful people still disagree. The European Randomized Study of Screening for Prostate Cancer, ERSPC, randomized about 182,000 men across seven countries to PSA screening roughly every four years or to usual care. At 13 years of follow-up it found a relative reduction in prostate cancer deaths of about 20 percent in the screened group — but because prostate cancer death is uncommon over such a window, the absolute numbers are sobering: on the order of 800 men needed to be invited to screening, and roughly 27 additional cancers diagnosed, to prevent one prostate cancer death, with the trade improving as follow-up lengthens. The Göteborg arm, which screened younger men every two years, showed a larger benefit — roughly a 40 percent relative mortality reduction — hinting that starting earlier and screening more often helps more. The American trial, PLCO, famously found no benefit, but its control group was so heavily contaminated — up to 90 percent of "unscreened" men actually had PSA tests through their own doctors — that it is now understood as comparing organized screening with widespread opportunistic screening, not with no screening. Against the benefit stand three well-documented harms. False positives: most men with an elevated PSA do not have cancer, yet many proceed to biopsy, with its anxiety, cost, and complications. Overdiagnosis: screening finds cancers — plausibly 20 to 50 percent of screen-detected ones under older practice — that would never have caused symptoms in the man's natural lifetime; each is a person told he has cancer who could not have benefited from knowing. Overtreatment: historically most such men were treated, and surgery and radiation carry lasting rates of urinary incontinence and erectile dysfunction, converting healthy men into patients. These arithmetic realities drove the United States Preventive Services Task Force to recommend against all PSA screening in 2012 — a grade D — after which screening and early diagnosis fell, and, with a lag, presentations with metastatic disease drifted upward; in 2018 the Task Force moved to a grade C for men 55 to 69: offer screening through individualized shared decision-making, and do not screen men 70 and older routinely. Two developments have genuinely shifted the balance since the trials were designed. Active surveillance — monitoring low-grade cancers instead of treating them — has become the standard for the harmless end of the spectrum, draining much of the overtreatment harm out of a positive screen. And MRI before biopsy filters out many men who once would have been biopsied needlessly. Screening in the 2020s is therefore a better bargain than the trial-era numbers suggest, but it remains a bargain with costs, and the honest framing is unchanged: screening trades a modest, real reduction in the chance of dying of prostate cancer for a meaningful chance of anxiety, procedures, and diagnoses you did not need.

sections.heading: Screening in Practice: Who, When, and How Often
sections.body: Turned into practical advice, modern screening looks like this. The decision is individual, and the conversation should happen while a man is healthy — ideally in his forties — rather than in the panic after a friend's diagnosis. For men at average risk, major guidelines converge on offering PSA-based screening between roughly ages 50 or 55 and 69, the range where trial evidence of benefit is strongest. For men at elevated risk — African ancestry, a father or brother with prostate cancer, or a known family mutation such as BRCA2 — the conversation moves earlier, to 40 or 45. A useful and underappreciated tool is the baseline PSA drawn in the forties: long-term Scandinavian data show that a man in his mid-forties whose PSA sits below the age-group median, around 0.7 to 1.0 ng/mL, has a very low lifetime risk of lethal prostate cancer and can safely stretch retesting to five-year intervals or longer, while a baseline in the top tenth marks the minority of men in whom most future deaths concentrate and who deserve regular follow-up. For men who choose ongoing screening, every one to two years is typical; every two to four years is defensible when values are low, since prostate cancer moves slowly and little is lost at the longer interval. Just as important is when to stop. Screening only helps a man likely to live long enough — commonly a decade or more — for a slow cancer to threaten him, so guidelines discourage routine screening beyond about 70, and more precisely beyond a remaining life expectancy of 10 to 15 years; a vigorous 72-year-old and a frail 66-year-old may sensibly make opposite choices, which is why age cutoffs are guides rather than rules. The digital rectal examination deserves honest framing: on its own it is a poor screening test — most early cancers cannot be felt — and guidelines no longer recommend it as a stand-alone screen, but it retains value alongside PSA because a distinctly hard, nodular, or asymmetric gland is suspicious regardless of the blood number, and the rare aggressive cancer that makes little PSA can announce itself only this way. Mechanics matter: draw the PSA before any gland manipulation, wait 48 to 72 hours after ejaculation, avoid testing during or shortly after a urinary infection, and note any finasteride or dutasteride use so the value can be doubled for interpretation. A man beginning screening should also decide, in advance and in writing to himself, what he will do with a mildly abnormal result — because the single most common failure of real-world screening is drift: a modestly elevated value, a plan to recheck that never happens, and a curable cancer found three years later. Finally, screening is a package deal only if you let it be: agreeing to a blood test does not commit a man to biopsy, and a diagnosis does not commit him to treatment. Each step is a separate decision, and knowing that in advance is what makes the first step reasonable.

sections.heading: From a High PSA to a Diagnosis: MRI and Biopsy
sections.body: A confirmed abnormal PSA sets off a sequence with decision points at every step, and the modern sequence differs importantly from the one a man's father experienced. Step one is always confirmation: repeat the test after several weeks, exclude infection, and correct for the known interfering factors — a large fraction of elevations disappear on retest, and no irreversible step should follow a single number. Step two, increasingly standard, is multiparametric MRI of the prostate before any needles. The scan combines anatomical and functional imaging — how water diffuses through tissue and how blood flows through it — and a radiologist scores any suspicious region on the PI-RADS scale from 1, almost certainly benign, to 5, highly suspicious. The landmark PRECISION trial in 2018 showed that using MRI to decide whom to biopsy, and where, detects more clinically significant cancers than the old blind approach while sparing roughly a quarter to a third of men biopsy altogether when the scan is clean — though a negative MRI does not reduce risk to zero, and a persistently rising PSA or high PSA density can still justify sampling. Risk calculators and secondary blood or urine markers can further refine the call for borderline cases. Step three is the biopsy itself, done under local anesthesia with a spring-loaded needle guided by ultrasound, typically taking 10 to 14 systematic cores from mapped regions of the gland plus extra targeted cores from any MRI lesion, fused onto the live ultrasound image by software or by the operator's eye. Route matters more than most men are told. The traditional transrectal route passes the needle through the rectal wall and inevitably drags some bacteria with it; even with antibiotic prophylaxis, roughly 1 to 3 percent of men develop serious infection, some septic. The transperineal route, through the skin behind the scrotum, nearly eliminates infectious risk and reaches the front of the gland better, and it has been displacing the transrectal approach; a man offered a transrectal biopsy is entitled to ask why. Expected aftermath either way includes blood in urine for days, blood in semen for weeks — alarming but harmless — and soreness; fever is not expected and means emergency care. Step four is pathology. If cancer is present, the report gives its grade, extent, and location; if not, the man is not entirely cleared — biopsies sample perhaps one two-thousandth of the gland — but a negative targeted biopsy after a quality MRI is genuinely reassuring, and follow-up usually returns to periodic PSA rather than reflexive re-biopsy. Only when a diagnosis is made does staging enter: for low-risk disease no further imaging is needed, while higher-risk disease is surveyed for spread, traditionally with a bone scan and CT and increasingly with PSMA PET — a scanner that lights up a surface molecule prostate cancer cells overexpress — which finds deposits those older scans miss. At every step the same principle holds: each test exists to answer a specific question, and a man is entitled to know, before agreeing, what question is being asked and what will change with the answer.

sections.heading: Reading the Pathology: Gleason Grades, Grade Groups, and Stage
sections.body: Two facts determine almost everything about a newly diagnosed prostate cancer's future: how abnormal its cells look and how far it has spread. The grading system is unique to this disease and worth understanding well enough to read your own report. In the 1960s the pathologist Donald Gleason observed that prostate cancers form recognizable architectural patterns and that a tumor's behavior tracks those patterns; his system, updated repeatedly since, scores the most common pattern in the tissue and the second most common, each on a scale where 3 represents recognizable but distorted glands, 4 represents fused and poorly formed glands, and 5 represents sheets of cells with almost no gland structure left. The two numbers are added, so scores run from 6, written 3+3, to 10, written 5+5. Notice the strange consequence: the lowest score modern pathologists actually assign is 6, which sounds ominously midway up a scale of 10 but is in fact the least aggressive category that exists — a source of endless unnecessary terror. To fix this, reporting since 2014 also uses Grade Groups 1 through 5: Grade Group 1 is Gleason 3+3, indolent disease that essentially never metastasizes while it remains pattern 3; Grade Group 2 is 3+4, mostly favorable with a minority of aggressive pattern; Grade Group 3 is 4+3, in which the aggressive pattern dominates; Grade Group 4 is Gleason 8; and Grade Group 5 is Gleason 9 or 10, the most dangerous end. The order of the numbers matters enormously — 3+4 and 4+3 both sum to 7 but carry meaningfully different prognoses — and the report will also note how many biopsy cores contained cancer and what percentage of each, which measures extent.
