Expressively, babbling becomes canonical — repeated consonant-vowel syllables such as bababa and dadada — by six to seven months, then takes on the intonation contours of the native language (jargoning). Gesture is a critical milestone in its own right: pointing to show things to another person, waving bye-bye, and giving objects to share attention emerge around nine to twelve months, and this joint attention is one of the strongest early markers whose absence raises concern for autism. First true words — used consistently and meaningfully — cluster around twelve months, with mama and dada used specifically slightly earlier. Red flags by twelve months: not sitting independently, no babbling, no pointing or gestures, not responding to name, no back-and-forth sharing of smiles, or failure to bear weight on the legs when held standing.

sections.heading: Twelve to Twenty-Four Months: Walking and the Word Explosion
sections.body: The second year delivers the two skills families remember forever: walking and talking. Independent walking arrives on average around twelve to thirteen months, but the normal range is famously wide — nine to seventeen or eighteen months — and within it, timing predicts nothing about later athletic or intellectual ability. A new walker toddles wide-based with arms held high for balance; within months the gait narrows, arms come down, and by eighteen months most toddlers run stiffly, stoop to pick things up without falling, climb onto furniture, and walk up steps with a hand held, one foot at a time. By twenty-four months they kick a ball, jump with both feet, and carry toys while walking. A child not walking at all by eighteen months needs evaluation, as does persistent toe-walking beyond about two years or any asymmetry of gait. Fine motor skills advance from a two-block tower at fifteen months to four to six blocks at eighteen to twenty-four months, scribbling spontaneously by fifteen to eighteen months, turning thick book pages, and using a spoon with moderate spill by eighteen months and fair competence by two. Language undergoes its most dramatic transformation. From roughly one to five words at twelve to fifteen months, vocabulary creeps to ten to twenty-five words around eighteen months — and then, for many children, explodes, with new words arriving daily. By twenty-four months the average expressive vocabulary is around 200 to 300 words, with 50 words the conventional minimum, and the defining milestone appears: two-word combinations such as more milk and daddy go, which mark the beginning of grammar. Comprehension runs far ahead throughout: an eighteen-month-old who says ten words may understand more than a hundred and can point to body parts and familiar pictures on request and follow one-step commands without gesture. A useful clinical rule: at age two, strangers should understand about half of what a child says; at three, about three quarters; at four, nearly everything. The late-talker question deserves honesty. A two-year-old with fewer than 50 words and no word combinations fits the definition; roughly half of such children catch up spontaneously by age three, but there is no reliable way to know in advance which half, and because hearing loss and autism hide in this group, the correct response is always a hearing test and a developmental evaluation rather than reassurance alone. Cognitively, toddlers use objects functionally (pushing a toy car, holding a phone to the ear), begin simple pretend play by eighteen months (feeding a doll), imitate chores, and solve problems by experimentation. Socially this is the era of parallel play beside rather than with peers, fierce autonomy, and the first tantrums, which are developmentally normal products of big desires and small language. Red flags: no single words by sixteen months, no two-word phrases by twenty-four months, no pretend play by eighteen to twenty-four months, loss of any language or social skill at any time.

sections.heading: Ages Two to Three: Language Takes Off and Play Turns Symbolic
sections.body: The third year of life converts a toddler into a conversationalist. Vocabulary grows from a few hundred words toward a thousand, and sentences stretch from two words to three, four, and five, acquiring the machinery of grammar along the way: plurals, the possessive, prepositions such as in and on, and the endlessly repeated questions what and where, followed late in the year by the first why. A three-year-old typically uses pronouns (I, me, you) mostly correctly, states first name and age, and is intelligible to strangers about 75 percent of the time. Normal disfluency deserves special mention because it frightens parents: many children between two and five repeat whole words and phrases — I want, I want, I want juice — especially when excited, and this ordinary developmental stuttering usually resolves on its own. Signs that instead suggest true stuttering worth evaluating include sound repetitions and prolongations (b-b-b-ball, mmmmilk), visible facial tension or struggle, avoidance of speaking, and persistence beyond six to twelve months or a family history of persistent stuttering. Motor development consolidates: a two-and-a-half-year-old jumps in place and walks on tiptoes on request; by three, children pedal a tricycle, alternate feet going up stairs, balance briefly on one foot, and catch a large ball against the chest. Fine motor control now supports copying a vertical line at two and a circle around three, building towers of eight to ten blocks, snipping with child-safe scissors, and turning single pages. Toilet training readiness typically arrives between twenty-four and thirty-six months — signaled by dry periods of two hours, awareness of a soiled diaper, ability to follow simple instructions, and interest — and daytime control is commonly achieved by three to four years, with nighttime dryness lagging as much as years behind; bed-wetting remains statistically normal to age five and beyond, affecting about 15 percent of five-year-olds and resolving spontaneously at roughly 15 percent per year thereafter. Cognitively, this is Piaget's early preoperational period: thinking is symbolic but intuitive, dominated by appearance rather than logic, and famously egocentric — not selfish, but literally limited in the ability to represent another person's viewpoint. Pretend play flowers from simple imitation into extended scenarios with substituted objects: a banana becomes a phone, a box becomes a boat. Socially, two-year-olds play alongside peers and begin brief cooperative exchanges by three; they know their own sex and age, insist on doing it myself, and swing between clinginess and independence. Tantrums peak in frequency between eighteen and thirty-six months — brief daily tantrums are within normal at this age — and fade as language gives frustration an outlet. Red flags for this period: no two-word phrases at twenty-four months, unintelligible to family at three, no pretend play, no interest in other children, inability to follow simple instructions, or frequent falling and difficulty with stairs at three.

sections.heading: The Preschool Years: Three to Five
sections.body: Between three and five, children become recognizably social beings with narratives, friends, rules, and theories about other minds. Gross motor skills mature toward adult patterns: a four-year-old hops on one foot, descends stairs with alternating feet, throws overhand with some accuracy, and catches a bounced ball; a five-year-old skips, balances on one foot for ten seconds, may pump a swing, and often learns to ride a bicycle with training wheels or, with practice, without. Fine motor progress is best tracked with a crayon: copying a circle at three, a cross at four, a square at four to four and a half, and a triangle around five; drawing a person progresses from a tadpole figure of head and legs at three to a six-part person by five. Most children establish stable hand dominance between two and four years. By five, children dress themselves, manage buttons, spread with a knife, and print some letters, often starting with their own name. Language reaches near-adult structure: a four-year-old speaks in five-to-six-word sentences, is fully intelligible to strangers, tells simple stories in sequence, uses past tense (with charming overregularizations such as goed and foots, which are actually evidence of rule learning, not errors of ignorance), and asks why relentlessly. By five, sentences are grammatically complete, vocabulary exceeds two thousand words, and children can count ten objects, name at least four colors, and understand time words such as yesterday and tomorrow. The cognitive headline of this period is theory of mind: around age four to five, children come to understand that other people can hold beliefs that are false. In the classic Sally-Anne experiment, a doll hides a marble, a second doll moves it while the first is away, and the child is asked where the returning doll will look; three-year-olds point to the marble's actual location, while most five-year-olds correctly predict she will look where she left it. This shift underwrites empathy, deception, joint pretense, and the complex social play — assigned roles, negotiated rules, imaginary friends (present in a substantial minority of children and entirely normal) — that dominates the preschool years. Play itself progresses through the sequence described by Mildred Parten: solitary, onlooker, parallel, associative, and finally genuinely cooperative play with shared goals by four to five. Fears of the dark, monsters, and separation are common and developmentally expected as imagination outruns reasoning. Growth is steady rather than dramatic — roughly 2 kilograms and 6 to 8 centimeters per year — and appetite is often erratic, which is normal so long as the growth curve holds. Red flags between three and five: speech unintelligible to strangers at four, no interest in interactive play, inability to separate from a caregiver by five without extreme distress, cannot copy a circle at four, cannot follow two-step instructions, ignores other children, or loses any previously acquired skill. School readiness by five includes attending to a task for five to ten minutes, following classroom-style directions, and managing toileting independently.

sections.heading: Middle Childhood: Six to Twelve
sections.body: Middle childhood, from roughly six to twelve, is growth's quiet plateau and cognition's great consolidation. Physical growth is the slowest and steadiest of the lifespan: about 5 to 6 centimeters and 2 to 3 kilograms per year, with body proportions elongating as limbs outgrow the trunk and baby fat recedes. The first permanent molars and lower incisors erupt around age six, beginning a tooth-replacement sequence of roughly four teeth per year that runs to about age twelve; twenty primary teeth are ultimately replaced and joined by permanent molars for a final count of up to thirty-two. Motor skills refine dramatically rather than appearing anew: running speed, balance, and coordination improve year over year, enabling organized sports by six to eight, and fine motor control matures from labored printing at six through fluent handwriting, and typically cursive capability, by eight to ten. A six-year-old's drawing shows a detailed person; by ten, perspective begins to appear. Cognitively, this is Piaget's stage of concrete operations, beginning around six to seven: children now conserve — they grasp that pouring water from a short wide glass into a tall thin one changes nothing about its amount — and they can classify along multiple dimensions, order objects by size, reverse operations mentally, and reason logically about concrete, tangible problems, while still struggling with purely abstract or hypothetical reasoning, which awaits adolescence. Memory strategy emerges: rehearsal around six to eight, organization and elaboration later, and metacognition — knowing what one knows — grows throughout. Academically, the canonical benchmarks are decoding print by six to seven with the often-quoted transition from learning to read toward reading to learn around third grade (age eight to nine), mastery of addition and subtraction facts by eight, multiplication tables by nine to ten, and fractions as the notorious hurdle of ten to twelve. Socially, the peer group becomes a developmental engine. Friendships shift from convenience to loyalty and shared values; children develop a stable self-concept built substantially on comparison with peers — Erik Erikson framed the period as industry versus inferiority, the stakes being a sense of competence — and rule-based games with negotiated fairness dominate play. Moral reasoning moves from rigid rule-following toward understanding intention and fairness. Most children develop a best friend, and by ten to twelve, cliques and early romantic interest appear. This is also the age at which learning and attention problems declare themselves under academic load: dyslexia affects roughly 5 to 10 percent of children and is signaled by persistent difficulty sounding out words despite adequate instruction; attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, affecting a similar share, requires symptoms in more than one setting beginning before age twelve. Red flags in middle childhood: reading substantially behind peers by seven to eight, inability to make or keep any friends, school refusal, marked clumsiness interfering with daily life (possible developmental coordination disorder), declining grades after earlier success, or persistent sadness, anxiety, or sleep disturbance, which in this age group are as significant as any motor delay was in infancy.

sections.heading: Puberty and the Adolescent Growth Spurt
sections.body: Puberty is the final act of childhood growth and the only time after infancy when growth accelerates. The sequence is initiated in the brain: the hypothalamus resumes pulsatile secretion of gonadotropin-releasing hormone, which drives the pituitary to release luteinizing and follicle-stimulating hormones, which in turn wake the gonads to produce estrogen or testosterone. Clinicians stage the visible results using the five Tanner stages, from stage 1 (prepubertal) to stage 5 (adult). In girls, the first sign is usually breast budding (thelarche), normally between ages 8 and 13, followed by pubic hair, the height spurt, and — on average about two to two and a half years after breast budding — menarche, the first menstrual period, at an average age of about 12.5 years in most well-nourished populations. In boys, the first sign is testicular enlargement (4 milliliters by orchidometer), normally between 9 and 14, followed by penile growth, pubic hair, the height spurt, voice change, and facial hair. The growth spurts are strikingly asymmetric in timing: girls hit peak height velocity of about 8 to 9 centimeters per year early in puberty, around age 11.5 to 12, while boys peak later, around 13.5 to 14, at about 9 to 10 centimeters per year — which is why girls tower over boys in early middle school and boys ultimately average about 13 centimeters taller, having grown for roughly two extra childhood years before a slightly larger spurt. Growth is limited by the skeleton itself: sex steroids, chiefly estrogen in both sexes, progressively fuse the cartilaginous growth plates, and after menarche most girls gain only about 5 to 7 centimeters more. Total pubertal gain averages around 25 centimeters in girls and 28 in boys. Weight, bone mass, and organs surge as well — nearly half of adult bone mineral is laid down during adolescence — and body composition diverges, girls adding proportionally more fat and boys more muscle. Timing varies widely and matters medically at the edges: evaluation is warranted for any pubertal signs before age 8 in girls or 9 in boys (precocious puberty), and for no breast development by 13, no menarche by 15 to 16, or no testicular enlargement by 14 (delayed puberty), the commonest cause of which is benign constitutional delay, though thyroid disease, undernutrition, intense athletic training, and chromosomal conditions such as Turner and Klinefelter syndromes must be considered. Gynecomastia — tender breast tissue in boys — occurs transiently in up to half of mid-pubertal males and usually resolves within one to two years. The brain undergoes its own puberty: limbic reward circuitry matures years before prefrontal control regions finish myelinating in the mid-twenties, a mismatch that helps explain adolescent risk appetite. Sleep phase shifts biologically later, while need remains 8 to 10 hours, a collision with early school start times that produces chronic adolescent sleep debt.

sections.heading: Language Development in Depth
sections.body: Language is the developmental stream most predictive of later academic life and the one most often delayed, so it repays a closer look at mechanism. Every hearing infant is born a universal listener, able to discriminate the phonemes of any human language; Patricia Kuhl's research showed that between about six and twelve months this ability narrows, with perception tuning to the native language — Japanese-learning infants, for example, losing the r/l distinction English preserves. Crucially, this tuning requires live social interaction: infants exposed to a foreign language by a present human retained discrimination, while matched exposure by video produced essentially no learning, a finding with obvious implications for screens. Statistical learning does heavy lifting: eight-month-olds track which syllables predictably follow which, using transition probabilities to find word boundaries in continuous speech after minutes of exposure. Adults unconsciously assist with infant-directed speech — the elevated pitch, stretched vowels, and exaggerated melody once dismissed as baby talk — which measurably aids segmentation and holds attention, and its use predicts vocabulary growth. Production climbs a fixed ladder: crying and vegetative sounds from birth, cooing at six to eight weeks, marginal babbling and raspberries at four to six months, canonical repeated syllables at six to eight months, jargoning with sentence-like melody at nine to twelve months, first words around twelve months, the vocabulary spurt often after roughly fifty words, two-word telegraphic speech at eighteen to twenty-four months, and grammatical morphemes — plural s, past tense ed, articles — in a remarkably consistent order described by Roger Brown across the third and fourth years. Overregularization errors (mouses, runned) appear precisely because the child has induced a rule, and they fade without correction; explicit grammar correction has little effect at this age, while recasting — repeating the child's utterance in correct form — quietly works. The quantity and quality of adult speech matter enormously. Hart and Risley's famous 1995 study estimated a gap of tens of millions of words heard by age three between the most- and least-talked-to children; the precise size of that gap has been contested by later replications, but the underlying finding — that conversational turns, not overheard background speech, predict language growth and even the strength of white-matter tracts such as the arcuate fasciculus — has held up robustly. Bilingualism deserves a clear myth correction: children exposed to two languages from birth hit major milestones (first words, two-word combinations) on the same schedule as monolinguals when both languages are counted; their vocabulary in each single language may measure smaller while the combined lexicon is equal or larger, and code-mixing within a sentence is a normal, rule-governed behavior, not confusion. Bilingual exposure does not cause language delay, and families should be advised to speak whichever languages they speak best and most naturally. Finally, comprehension always leads production, and a child who understands well but speaks late has a meaningfully better prognosis than one who neither understands nor speaks — though both deserve a hearing test first, always.

sections.heading: Developmental Screening, Surveillance, and Red Flags
sections.body: Because parents adapt to their own child and comparison samples are small, structured screening catches problems that informal impressions miss, and health systems have built scheduled checkpoints for exactly this reason. Surveillance — asking about skills, watching the child, tracking growth — happens at every visit, while formal screening uses validated questionnaires at set ages: in the widely followed American Academy of Pediatrics schedule, general developmental screening at 9, 18, and 30 months and autism-specific screening at 18 and 24 months. The workhorse general tools are parent-completed questionnaires such as the Ages and Stages Questionnaires (ASQ-3) and the PEDS, which take minutes and perform about as well as clinician-administered instruments like the Denver Developmental Screening Test that they have largely replaced. Autism screening at 18 and 24 months typically uses the M-CHAT-R/F, a twenty-question checklist probing joint attention, pretend play, response to name, and eye contact, with a structured follow-up interview that sharply reduces false positives. In 2022 the CDC revised its public milestone checklists from 50th-percentile ages (what half of children do) to 75th-percentile ages (what three quarters do), so that a missed checklist item now genuinely means act rather than wait — a change worth knowing because older and newer lists disagree by a month or two on purpose. A compact set of red flags is worth committing to memory. Motor: not rolling by 6 months, not sitting unsupported by 9, not bearing weight on legs by 12, not walking by 18, hand preference before 18 months, persistent toe-walking after 2 years, or persistent primitive reflexes past 6 months. Language and hearing: no babbling by 9 to 12 months, no response to name by 12 months, no first words by 16 months, fewer than 50 words or no two-word phrases by 24 months, unintelligible to strangers at 4 years, or any parental suspicion of hearing loss at any age. Social and cognitive: no social smile by 3 months, no joint-attention pointing by 12 to 15 months, no pretend play by 18 to 24 months, no interest in other children by 3 years. Growth: weight or height crossing two major percentile lines in either direction, head circumference crossing percentiles, or body mass index above the 95th percentile. And the universal rule that overrides every table: regression — loss of previously mastered words, social engagement, or motor skills — is a red flag at any age and warrants prompt evaluation, as it can signal autism with regression, seizure disorders such as Landau-Kleffner syndrome, or metabolic and neurodegenerative disease. When screening flags a concern, the correct next steps run in parallel, not sequence: audiology referral (hearing loss is the great imitator of every developmental problem), referral for diagnostic evaluation, and referral to early intervention services, which in many countries — including the United States under IDEA Part C — do not require a diagnosis to begin before age three. Waiting to see is the one option the evidence does not support.

sections.heading: Nutrition, Sleep, and Everyday Inputs That Drive Growth
sections.body: Growth and development run on inputs a household controls: food, sleep, movement, and interaction. Nutrition comes first. The World Health Organization recommends exclusive breastfeeding for about the first six months, with iron-fortified formula the standard substitute; either way, breastfed infants need a daily vitamin D supplement of 400 international units, because human milk contains little, and all infants need an external iron source by around six months as the iron endowment from birth runs out — iron-fortified cereals, meat, or legumes matter here, since iron-deficiency anemia in infancy is associated with lasting cognitive effects. Solid foods begin around six months, when the infant sits with support, has lost the tongue-thrust reflex, and shows interest; current allergy science, led by the 2015 LEAP trial, reversed decades of advice by showing that early introduction of peanut protein (as thinned butter or puffs, never whole nuts) between four and eleven months cut peanut allergy by roughly 80 percent in high-risk infants — delay, not early exposure, is the risk. Whole cow's milk waits until twelve months (it is low in iron and hard on infant kidneys), honey waits until twelve months because of infant botulism spores, and choking hazards — whole grapes, nuts, popcorn, chunks of hot dog — wait until at least four years or are cut small. Toddler appetite falls sharply after the first year as growth slows; a two-year-old genuinely needs only around 1,000 to 1,200 kilocalories a day, and the erratic, food-refusing toddler whose growth curve is steady is normal. The most common nutritional saboteur at this age is liquid: more than about 500 milliliters of milk or any habitual juice displaces iron-rich food and calories. Sleep is the second pillar, with consensus recommendations per 24 hours of 14 to 17 hours for newborns, 12 to 16 for infants four to twelve months, 11 to 14 for ages one to two, 10 to 13 for three to five, 9 to 12 for six to twelve, and 8 to 10 for teenagers; growth hormone is secreted predominantly in deep slow-wave sleep, and chronic short sleep in childhood is linked to attention, mood, and weight problems. Safe-sleep practice for the first year — alone, on the back, in a bare crib — remains the single most effective sudden-infant-death precaution. Movement and interaction close the loop: infants need supervised prone play daily; toddlers and preschoolers need three hours of varied physical activity spread across the day; school-age children need an hour of moderate-to-vigorous activity daily. For screens, major pediatric bodies converge on avoiding screen media (other than video chat) before 18 to 24 months, a one-hour daily ceiling of high-quality content co-viewed with an adult from two to five, and consistent family rules thereafter — grounded in the evidence that young children learn language from responsive humans, poorly from video alone. None of these inputs requires money so much as regularity: the same foods offered patiently (ten or more exposures before a new food is accepted is typical), the same bedtime, and daily back-and-forth conversation and reading, which remain the best-documented boosters of language and school readiness available at any price.

sections.heading: Variation, Prematurity, and the Limits of Milestone Checklists
sections.body: Every table in this guide describes populations, and honest use of it requires knowing where individual children legitimately depart from the averages. Prematurity is the most common systematic case. A baby born at 28 weeks' gestation who is now six months old has really had only three months of expected development; the rule is to correct for prematurity — assess milestones and plot growth against corrected age (chronological age minus the weeks missed before 40) — until at least 24 months, by which point most healthy preterm children have caught up. Judging a preemie against uncorrected age manufactures false delays and needless alarm. Genetic background produces equally legitimate variation: children of short parents track low percentiles healthily (familial short stature, with normal growth velocity and bone age), and constitutional growth delay produces late-blooming adolescents who end at normal height. Some cultural and practice effects are real but transient — infants who sleep on their backs and get little tummy time roll and crawl somewhat later; children carried constantly may walk a few weeks later — without any effect on eventual outcomes. Certain conditions require their own reference standards entirely, with dedicated growth charts for Down syndrome, Turner syndrome, and achondroplasia. It is also worth stating what milestones cannot do. They are weak predictors at the individual level within the normal range: the age of first steps does not forecast athletic ability, and early talking only loosely predicts later verbal skill. Checklists sample behavior at a moment — a tired, hungry, or wary child performs below ability, which is why screening tools rely on parent report across settings and why one bad clinic visit should never carry a diagnosis. Milestone instruments were normed mostly on Western populations, and cross-cultural research shows real spread: some African infant-care traditions that deliberately exercise stepping are associated with walking weeks earlier than European norms, while some swaddling-heavy traditions shift motor milestones later, all within healthy development. Conversely, limits cut the other way: passing a screen does not guarantee typical development, and persistent parental concern has repeatedly been shown to be one of the most sensitive indicators available, so a normal score should never be used to dismiss a parent who says something is wrong. When development does go wrong, outcomes hinge on speed of response. The practical algorithm is short: any red flag or strong parental concern leads to a hearing test, a formal developmental evaluation, and enrollment in early-intervention services immediately and in parallel — therapy for a delay never harms a child who would have caught up anyway, while waiting squanders the years of maximal brain plasticity. Families should keep their own records (dated notes or videos of new skills beat memory), bring them to visits, and treat the growth chart and milestone history the way a pilot treats instruments: not as a verdict on the child, but as the earliest, cheapest, and kindest warning system medicine has.

guides.safetyNote: Milestone ages are population landmarks, not deadlines; wide variation is normal. But loss of previously acquired skills, absent response to sound, fever of 38.0 C (100.4 F) or higher in a baby under three months, or a bulging fontanelle warrant prompt medical evaluation. When in doubt about a delay, seek a hearing test and professional assessment early rather than waiting.

guides.title: Newborn Care Basics for New Parents
guides.summary: A comprehensive practical guide to caring for a baby in the first weeks of life, covering feeding, sleep, diapering, cord and skin care, normal newborn appearance and vital signs, and the specific warning signs that mean a newborn needs medical attention immediately.

sections.heading: The First Six Weeks: What You Are Actually Dealing With
sections.body:
A newborn is conventionally defined as a baby in the first 28 days of life, though the practical adjustment period for a household runs closer to six or eight weeks. The single most useful thing to understand at the outset is that a healthy newborn is not a small child. It is a physiologically distinct creature that has just completed the most abrupt transition it will ever make: from a warm, dark, fluid-filled space where oxygen and nutrition arrived continuously through the umbilical cord, to a cold, bright, dry world where it must breathe, thermoregulate, digest, and signal its needs entirely on its own. Almost everything that alarms new parents in the first month is a normal feature of that transition rather than a sign of illness. Almost everything that genuinely is dangerous announces itself through a short, learnable list of signs.

Newborn stomach capacity on day one is roughly the size of a cherry, about five to seven millilitres. By day three it holds around twenty-two to twenty-seven millilitres, and by the end of the first week roughly forty-five to sixty millilitres. This is why a newborn feeds eight to twelve times in twenty-four hours and why a parent who expects a baby to take a large meal and sleep for four hours will conclude, wrongly, that something is broken. The stomach is small and breast milk in particular empties from it in about ninety minutes. Frequent feeding is the design, not a malfunction.

Sleep follows a similarly unfamiliar pattern. Newborns sleep fourteen to seventeen hours per twenty-four, but in fragments of thirty minutes to four hours, distributed with no regard for day or night, because the circadian system that will eventually consolidate sleep does not begin producing meaningful melatonin rhythms until roughly eight to twelve weeks. There is no technique that reliably makes a two-week-old sleep through the night, and any product or method promising this should be treated with suspicion.

The realistic goal for the first six weeks is therefore not to establish routines, train behaviours, or optimise anything. It is to keep the baby fed, warm, clean, and safely positioned, to notice the small number of signs that require a clinician, and to keep the adults functional enough to continue doing all of that. Weight gain and output are the two objective measures that tell you feeding is working. A baby who is back to birth weight by two weeks, producing six or more wet nappies a day, and alert and rousable when awake is almost certainly fine, regardless of how much it cries or how little it sleeps. Holding those two anchors in mind converts an overwhelming period into a manageable one, and gives you a concrete answer when well-meaning advice from six different sources contradicts itself.

sections.heading: Normal Newborn Appearance, Reflexes and Vital Signs
sections.body:
A newborn straight from a vaginal birth often looks alarming to someone who has only seen photographs of month-old babies. The skull bones are not fused and overlap during passage through the birth canal, producing moulding that leaves the head cone-shaped for a few days. A caput succedaneum is a soft, boggy swelling of the scalp that crosses suture lines and resolves within days. A cephalohaematoma is a firmer collection of blood under the periosteum that does not cross suture lines, appears over the first day or two, and may take weeks to reabsorb; it can raise bilirubin levels as it breaks down. The soft spots, or fontanelles, are normal: the diamond-shaped anterior fontanelle closes between nine and eighteen months, the smaller posterior one by about two months. A flat, softly pulsating fontanelle is normal. A sunken one suggests dehydration and a tensely bulging one in a quiet, upright baby suggests raised pressure inside the skull and needs urgent assessment.

The skin produces the largest crop of harmless findings. Vernix caseosa is the white waxy coating that protected the skin in utero. Lanugo is fine downy body hair, more abundant in babies born earlier. Milia are tiny white keratin cysts across the nose and cheeks that vanish without treatment. Erythema toxicum neonatorum, an unfortunate name for a completely benign rash, appears in around half of term babies as blotchy red patches with small pale centres that migrate around the body over days. Congenital dermal melanocytosis produces slate-grey patches over the lower back and buttocks, most commonly in babies with darker skin, and is not bruising. Salmon patches on the eyelids, glabella and nape are dilated capillaries that fade over months. Peeling and cracking, especially at the wrists and ankles, is normal desquamation. Blue hands and feet, called acrocyanosis, are normal for the first day or two; blueness of the lips, tongue and central face is never normal and demands immediate attention.

Vital signs sit in ranges that would be abnormal in an adult. Heart rate runs 120 to 160 beats per minute at rest, briefly reaching 180 or more when crying and dipping to 90 or so in deep sleep. Respiratory rate is 30 to 60 breaths per minute and is normally irregular: periodic breathing, in which the baby breathes rapidly, pauses for five to ten seconds, then resumes, is normal. A pause longer than twenty seconds, or any pause with colour change or limpness, is apnoea and is not. Normal temperature is 36.5 to 37.5 degrees Celsius, or 97.7 to 99.5 Fahrenheit.

Primitive reflexes are the neurological examination made visible. The Moro or startle reflex, in which the arms fling outward then draw back in, indicates intact brainstem pathways and fades by three to six months. Rooting turns the head toward a touched cheek; sucking, palmar grasp, plantar grasp, the stepping reflex and the asymmetric tonic neck or fencing posture all belong to the same repertoire and all disappear on schedule as voluntary movement takes over.

sections.heading: Breastfeeding: Mechanism, Latch and Establishing Supply
sections.body:
Milk production runs on a hormonal switch followed by a supply-and-demand loop, and understanding the two phases explains most early breastfeeding trouble. During pregnancy, high circulating progesterone from the placenta blocks the milk-producing effect of prolactin. Delivery of the placenta causes progesterone to collapse within hours, which releases that brake and triggers lactogenesis II, the copious milk production commonly described as milk coming in. This typically happens between thirty and seventy-two hours after birth, later after a caesarean, a difficult delivery, significant blood loss, or in mothers with diabetes or obesity. Before that point the breast produces colostrum: a thick, yellow, low-volume, protein- and antibody-rich fluid delivered in quantities of two to ten millilitres per feed. That looks like nothing in a bottle and is exactly right for a stomach the size of a cherry.

After the first week, production is governed almost entirely by removal. Milk contains a protein called feedback inhibitor of lactation, which accumulates in a full breast and suppresses further synthesis. Emptying the breast washes the inhibitor away and production accelerates. This is why frequent, effective removal builds supply and why long gaps, scheduled feeding, or routine top-ups with formula in the early weeks tend to reduce it. Oxytocin, released in response to suckling and to the sight, sound or smell of the baby, contracts the muscle cells around the milk-producing alveoli and pushes milk down the ducts, the let-down reflex, often felt as tingling and sometimes accompanied by strong uterine cramping in the first days.

Latch is the mechanical part and the part most worth getting right. The baby should take a large mouthful of breast tissue, not just the nipple, with the nipple drawn far back toward the junction of the hard and soft palate where it is not compressed. Signs of a good latch are a widely open mouth, lips flanged outward, more areola visible above the upper lip than below the lower, the chin pressed into the breast, the nose clear, and rhythmic sucking that changes after the first minute from rapid fluttering to a slow deep suck-swallow-breathe pattern with audible swallows. Pain is the key diagnostic. A few seconds of discomfort as the baby draws the nipple in is common; sustained pain through the feed, or a nipple that emerges flattened, creased or lipstick-shaped, means the latch is shallow and should be broken by slipping a clean finger into the corner of the mouth and started again.

Expect eight to twelve feeds in twenty-four hours, including at least one or two overnight, since prolactin levels are highest at night. Cluster feeding, in which a baby demands the breast almost continuously for several hours, usually in the evening and especially around days two to three, weeks two to three and six weeks, is normal supply-signalling behaviour and is not evidence of insufficient milk.

sections.heading: Formula Feeding and Safe Bottle Preparation
sections.body:
Infant formula is a regulated food designed to approximate human milk in energy density, at roughly sixty-seven kilocalories per hundred millilitres, or twenty kilocalories per fluid ounce. Standard cow's milk-based formula suits the overwhelming majority of babies. Hydrolysed and amino-acid formulas exist for diagnosed cow's milk protein allergy, which affects only two to three percent of infants. Never dilute formula to stretch it: over-dilution causes water intoxication, hyponatraemia and seizures, and has killed babies. Never make it stronger than directed either, which loads the immature kidney with excess solute.

The critical safety point is that powdered infant formula is not a sterile product. It is pasteurised but can carry Cronobacter sakazakii and Salmonella; infection is rare but devastating, causing meningitis and sepsis with reported mortality of forty to eighty percent. Babies under three months, born preterm, or immunocompromised are at highest risk, and for them the World Health Organization advises reconstituting powder with water boiled and then cooled to no lower than seventy degrees Celsius, which kills Cronobacter, then cooling the bottle rapidly before feeding. Ready-to-feed liquid formula is commercially sterile and is the safest option for a vulnerable baby.

Timing rules matter as much as temperature. A freshly prepared bottle left at room temperature should be discarded after two hours, and once a baby has begun drinking, saliva introduces bacteria and the remainder must go within one hour. Prepared formula kept at four degrees Celsius or below lasts twenty-four hours; expressed breast milk keeps four hours at room temperature, four days refrigerated, six months frozen. Never warm a bottle in a microwave, which produces superheated pockets that scald the mouth even when the outside feels cool. When feeding, hold the baby fairly upright, keep the bottle close to horizontal so the teat fills only partly, and pause every twenty to thirty sucks. Typical intake after the first week is around 150 to 180 millilitres per kilogram of body weight daily, but babies self-regulate and one who turns away has finished. Never leave a baby unattended with a propped bottle.
steps: Wash your hands with soap and water and clean the surface you will work on.
Sterilise bottles, teats, rings and caps by boiling for five minutes fully submerged, by steam steriliser, or in cold-water sterilising solution.
Boil fresh drinking water and let it stand no more than thirty minutes, so it is still above seventy degrees Celsius when it meets the powder.
Pour the exact volume of hot water in first, reading the graduations at eye level; adding powder first displaces water and over-concentrates the feed.
Add the stated number of level scoops using only that tin's scoop, levelling each with a clean knife rather than packing it down.
Cap the bottle and shake until no lumps remain against the light.
Cool rapidly under cold running water or in a jug of iced water, keeping the water level below the cap.
Shake a few drops onto your inner wrist; it should feel neutral, neither warm nor cool.
Feed within two hours of preparation, and discard any milk left one hour after the baby first drank from it.

sections.heading: Reading Hunger Cues, Feeding Adequacy and Weight
sections.body:
Crying is a late hunger cue. By the time a newborn is crying it is usually distressed enough that latching becomes harder, so learning the earlier signals makes feeding markedly easier. The sequence runs roughly: stirring and eye movement under closed lids, mouth opening, head turning and rooting, hands moving to the mouth, increasing body movement and fussing, and only then full crying with a red face and flailing limbs. Offering the breast or bottle in the rooting phase is a different experience from offering it to a screaming baby. If a baby is already crying hard, calming first with skin-to-skin contact and rocking for a minute or two usually produces a better feed than fighting to latch a rigid, distressed infant.

Because you cannot see how much a breastfed baby has taken, feeding adequacy is judged indirectly from four converging pieces of evidence: output, weight, behaviour and the sensation at the breast. Output follows a reliable schedule in the first week. Expect roughly one wet nappy on day one, two on day two, three on day three, and from around day five onward at least six heavy wet nappies in twenty-four hours, with urine that is pale and near-odourless. Stools progress from meconium, which is black, sticky and tar-like, through greenish-brown transitional stool around days three and four, to the mustard-yellow, seedy, loose stool of an established milk feed by day five. At least three or four such stools daily in the first month is reassuring. Brick-dust-coloured urate crystals in the nappy are common in the first two or three days but after day three suggest underfeeding.

Weight is the objective anchor. Almost all newborns lose weight after birth, mostly as extracellular fluid, and a loss of up to seven percent of birth weight is unremarkable while up to ten percent is generally tolerated with closer watching. Loss beyond ten percent, or continuing loss after day five, calls for a feeding assessment the same day. Babies should regain birth weight by ten to fourteen days and then gain roughly twenty-five to thirty-five grams per day, about one ounce, for the first three months. A single weight is far less informative than a trend on a growth chart, and clothing, scale differences and a full or empty bladder introduce enough noise that a fifty-gram discrepancy should not be over-interpreted.

Behaviour completes the picture. A well-fed newborn comes off the breast relaxed with open hands and an unclenched jaw, has periods of quiet alertness during the day, and is easy to rouse. Warning combinations are a baby who is consistently sleepy and difficult to wake for feeds, feeds for very long stretches without audible swallowing and then remains unsettled, has fewer than six wet nappies after day five, or shows persistent jaundice with poor feeding. Those warrant a clinical review rather than another week of waiting to see.

sections.heading: Nappies, Elimination and Nappy Rash
sections.body:
A newborn will go through eight to twelve nappy changes a day, and the routine is worth making efficient because you will perform it roughly two thousand times in the first six months. The core principles are simple: change promptly when soiled, clean front to back to avoid dragging faecal bacteria toward the urethra, dry thoroughly because moisture is what breaks skin down, and never turn away from a baby on a raised surface even for a second, since rolling appears without warning and falls from changing tables are a common preventable injury.

For cleaning, plain warm water and cotton wool or a soft cloth is entirely adequate in the first weeks and is gentler than most wipes. If you use wipes, choose fragrance-free and alcohol-free ones. In boys, do not retract the foreskin, which is normally fused to the glans in infancy and can be damaged and scarred by forcible retraction; simply wipe the outside. Point the penis downward inside the nappy to reduce leaks upward. In girls, wipe the outer labia only and do not clean inside them; a small amount of white discharge, and even a few days of blood-streaked mucus around days three to seven, is normal pseudomenstruation caused by withdrawal of maternal oestrogen, and needs no treatment.

Nappy rash is usually irritant contact dermatitis: prolonged contact with urine raises skin pH, faecal enzymes then digest the surface layer, and friction completes the damage. It shows as red, sometimes shiny or eroded skin on the convex surfaces, the buttocks and the tops of the thighs, characteristically sparing the depths of the skin creases. Treatment is more nappy-free air time, changing at shorter intervals, and a thick barrier of zinc oxide or petrolatum applied like icing rather than rubbed in. Candida nappy rash looks different and is the important distinction: beefy red, involving the creases rather than sparing them, with small satellite spots at the margins, and it does not respond to barrier cream alone but needs a topical antifungal such as clotrimazole or nystatin.

Elimination patterns cause enormous unnecessary worry. Exclusively breastfed babies past the first month may stool after every feed or, entirely normally, only once every five to seven days, because breast milk is so completely absorbed that there is little residue. What matters is that the stool, when it comes, is soft. Straining, grunting, going red and drawing up the legs while passing a soft stool is infant dyschezia, an immature coordination of pushing and relaxing the pelvic floor, and it resolves without intervention. Genuine constipation means hard, pellet-like stools. Three findings are never normal and require prompt medical review: no meconium passed within the first forty-eight hours, which raises the question of Hirschsprung disease or obstruction; frank blood or currant-jelly stool; and white, chalky or pale putty-coloured stool, which can indicate biliary atresia, a condition where surgical outcomes depend heavily on diagnosis within the first sixty days of life.

sections.heading: Umbilical Cord Care, Bathing and Newborn Skin
sections.body:
The umbilical stump is dead tissue that separates by a process of dry gangrene and leucocyte infiltration. It typically darkens from yellowish-white to brown-black over several days and detaches somewhere between day five and day fifteen, most commonly around day seven to ten, occasionally as late as three weeks. A few drops of blood at separation and a small amount of sticky, slightly smelly moisture at the base are normal. Current guidance in settings with clean water and low infection rates is dry cord care: keep the stump clean and dry, expose it to air, fold the nappy down below it, and do not apply alcohol, antiseptic powders or ointments, which delay separation without reducing infection. In settings with high neonatal mortality and unhygienic delivery conditions, the World Health Organization instead recommends a single daily application of 7.1 percent chlorhexidine digluconate for the first week, which reduces omphalitis and neonatal death.

Omphalitis, infection of the cord stump, is uncommon but progresses fast in a newborn. The signs are redness of the skin spreading outward from the base more than about five millimetres, swelling and warmth, frank pus rather than sticky discharge, a foul odour, bleeding that does not stop, or any accompanying fever or poor feeding. That combination is a same-day medical problem. A soft pink lump of moist tissue remaining after separation is usually an umbilical granuloma, which is harmless and treated simply in clinic. A soft bulge under the navel that pushes out when the baby cries is an umbilical hernia; the great majority close spontaneously by age three to five and should never be taped, strapped or bound with a coin.

Bathing is largely a comfort activity in the first weeks, not a hygiene necessity. Newborn skin has a thin stratum corneum and an acidic surface film that supports the barrier and resists pathogens, and over-washing with soap strips both. Two or three baths a week is plenty, with the nappy area and neck creases cleaned daily. Until the cord separates, most clinicians suggest sponge bathing rather than immersion. Water temperature should be 37 to 38 degrees Celsius, about 98 to 100 Fahrenheit. Test it with your elbow or the inside of your wrist rather than your hand, which is far less sensitive, and fill the bath before putting the baby in so that a hot tap can never run onto the skin. Setting the household water heater to 49 degrees Celsius, 120 Fahrenheit, gives a margin against scalding: at 60 degrees a full-thickness burn takes about five seconds, at 49 degrees it takes around ten minutes.

Never leave a baby unattended in bath water even momentarily, and never with an older sibling as the only supervision. Infant drowning can occur in a few centimetres of water and is silent. Use one hand to support the head and neck at all times, keep the bath short, and dry the skin folds properly afterward. If the skin is dry or cracking, a plain fragrance-free emollient is more useful than baby oil products containing perfume, and delaying skincare additives reduces the chance of sensitisation.

sections.heading: Sleep and the Evidence Behind Safe Sleep Practice
sections.body:
Newborn sleep is structurally different from adult sleep. About half of it is active sleep, the precursor of rapid eye movement sleep, during which babies twitch, grimace, whimper, breathe irregularly and open their eyes briefly. Parents routinely mistake active sleep for waking and intervene, converting a sleeping baby into an awake one. Sleep cycles last only forty to fifty minutes against ninety in adults, and babies enter through active sleep rather than deep sleep, which is why a baby who seems asleep in your arms wakes the instant they are set down: they were not yet in quiet sleep. Waiting until the limbs go floppy and breathing becomes deep and regular, usually about twenty minutes after falling asleep, dramatically improves the odds of a successful transfer.

The safe sleep recommendations exist because of a body of epidemiological evidence that is unusually strong for a public health intervention. Sudden infant death syndrome rates in participating countries fell by roughly fifty to ninety percent after back-to-sleep campaigns beginning around 1991 to 1994. The mechanism is thought to involve a vulnerable infant with immature arousal responses, at a critical developmental period around two to four months, exposed to an external stressor such as rebreathing exhaled carbon dioxide trapped near the face, overheating, or airway obstruction. Prone sleeping raises the risk several fold; soft bedding, sleeping on sofas or armchairs, and exposure to tobacco smoke all raise it further.

The practical rules are compact. Always place a baby on the back for every sleep, including naps, from the first day. Side-lying is not a safe alternative because babies roll prone from it. Use a firm, flat, separate sleep surface with a fitted sheet and nothing else in it: no pillows, duvets, quilts, bumpers, positioners, wedges, or soft toys. Room-share without bed-sharing, keeping the cot or bassinet in the parents' room, for at least the first six months, which is associated with a substantially lower risk. Keep the room comfortably cool, around 16 to 20 degrees Celsius, and dress the baby in one more thin layer than you find comfortable rather than heavy bedding; a sleeping bag of appropriate tog is safer than blankets. Avoid smoking in pregnancy and around the baby. Offer a pacifier at sleep onset once feeding is established, which is consistently associated with reduced risk for reasons that remain incompletely explained.

Sofas and armchairs deserve particular emphasis because falling asleep with a baby on one carries a risk of death estimated at up to fifty times that of a safe cot. A parent who realises they may doze while feeding at night is safer feeding in a bed cleared of pillows and duvets than on a sofa. Car seats, swings and bouncers are not sleep surfaces: a newborn's head can fall forward and obstruct the airway, a phenomenon called positional asphyxia, so a sleeping baby who arrives home in a car seat should be moved to a flat surface, and total time in a seat should be limited.

sections.heading: Crying, Soothing and the Reality of Colic
sections.body:
Crying follows a predictable developmental curve that was characterised by the paediatrician Ronald Barr and is sometimes taught as the period of purple crying. Crying increases from birth, peaks at around six to eight weeks of age at an average of two to three hours in twenty-four, and then declines through three to four months. The peak occurs across cultures and feeding methods, in preterm babies corrected for gestational age, and in babies who are carried constantly. It clusters in the late afternoon and evening, is often unrelated to any identifiable cause, resists soothing during the episode, and ends as abruptly as it began. Knowing this is protective: parents who understand that peak crying is normal and self-limiting are less likely to conclude that they are failing or that the baby is ill, and less likely to reach the point of desperation that precedes shaking.

Colic is the label applied when this normal crying is at the extreme end. The traditional Wessel criteria are crying for more than three hours a day, more than three days a week, for more than three weeks, in an otherwise thriving baby. It affects roughly one in five infants. Despite decades of investigation, no single cause has been established; candidate explanations include immature gut motility, transient lactase insufficiency, differences in gut microbiota, cow's milk protein sensitivity in a minority, and simple variation in temperament. The honest position is that for most babies the cause is unknown and no treatment has robust evidence. Simethicone does not outperform placebo, and gripe waters are unregulated. Some trials of Lactobacillus reuteri show modest benefit in breastfed infants, with inconsistent replication. A two-week trial of maternal dairy elimination, or a hydrolysed formula, is reasonable if there are other allergy signs such as blood in the stool or eczema.

Practical soothing works by reproducing the sensory environment of late gestation. Swaddling firmly around the arms but loosely around the hips, so the legs can flex and abduct, restrains the startle reflex; swaddling must stop as soon as the baby shows any sign of rolling, and a swaddle that binds the legs straight increases the risk of hip dysplasia. Side or stomach positioning while held and awake, a loud continuous shushing at roughly the volume of the baby's own cry, rhythmic jiggling of small amplitude, and sucking on a breast, finger or pacifier are the components popularised by Harvey Karp and they do help many babies. So does skin-to-skin contact, a walk outdoors, a warm bath, and reducing stimulation in a dim quiet room.

The most important instruction in this whole subject is what to do when nothing works. Put the baby down on their back in a safe cot, walk out of the room, and let them cry for five or ten minutes while you breathe, call someone, or stand outside. A crying baby in a safe cot comes to no harm. Shaking a baby, even briefly, causes abusive head trauma with retinal and subdural bleeding, and kills or permanently disables a large proportion of its victims. Every parent should have a rehearsed plan for that moment before it arrives.

sections.heading: Jaundice: Why It Happens and When It Is Dangerous
sections.body:
Roughly sixty percent of term newborns and eighty percent of preterm newborns become visibly yellow in the first week, making jaundice the most common reason a healthy-looking newborn is readmitted to hospital. The mechanism is a predictable consequence of birth. Fetal red blood cells last about seventy to ninety days rather than the adult one hundred and twenty, and the newborn starts with a high haematocrit that must fall. Breaking down that haemoglobin releases haem, which is converted to unconjugated bilirubin, a yellow, fat-soluble pigment. The liver must attach glucuronic acid to it using an enzyme called UGT1A1 to make it water-soluble and excretable, and newborn activity of that enzyme is only about one percent of adult levels at birth, reaching adult levels at around fourteen weeks. Meanwhile the gut reabsorbs bilirubin through enterohepatic circulation, particularly when feeding is slow to establish and stooling is infrequent.

This physiological jaundice appears after twenty-four hours, peaks at around day three to five in term babies and day five to seven in preterm babies, and fades over one to two weeks. It progresses in a cephalocaudal direction, appearing first in the face and sclerae and moving down the trunk and finally to the palms and soles as levels rise, which gives a crude bedside estimate, especially unreliable in babies with darker skin where visual assessment underestimates severity. Levels are properly measured by transcutaneous bilirubinometer or serum bilirubin, plotted against age in hours on a nomogram, since the treatment threshold at twenty-four hours is far lower than at ninety-six hours.

Three patterns signal pathology rather than physiology. Jaundice appearing in the first twenty-four hours of life is always abnormal and usually indicates haemolysis, from ABO or Rhesus incompatibility, glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, or hereditary spherocytosis. Jaundice that is severe or rising more than about 0.2 milligrams per decilitre per hour needs urgent measurement. Jaundice persisting beyond two weeks in a term baby, or accompanied by pale chalky stools and dark urine, requires a split bilirubin measurement to look for conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, because biliary atresia is treatable if operated on early and disastrous if missed.

The reason any of this matters is kernicterus. Unconjugated bilirubin unbound to albumin crosses the blood-brain barrier and is toxic to the basal ganglia and brainstem nuclei, producing acute bilirubin encephalopathy, which begins with lethargy and poor feeding and progresses through a high-pitched cry, arching of the neck and back, and fever, to chronic athetoid cerebral palsy, hearing loss and permanent gaze palsy. It is now rare precisely because it is screened for and treated. Treatment is phototherapy, in which blue light at roughly 460 to 490 nanometres converts bilirubin in the skin into water-soluble isomers that are excreted without the liver's help; it is safe and effective. Exchange transfusion is reserved for extreme levels. Sunlight through a window is not a substitute and risks burns and hypothermia. The most useful thing a parent can do is feed frequently, since milk intake and stooling clear bilirubin through the gut, and seek measurement rather than reassurance when a baby looks more yellow than yesterday, particularly if also sleepy and feeding poorly.

sections.heading: Temperature, Fever and the Newborn Emergency List
sections.body:
Newborns thermoregulate badly. They have a surface area roughly three times greater than an adult's relative to body mass, thin subcutaneous fat, and no ability to shiver effectively. Their main defence against cold is non-shivering thermogenesis, in which brown adipose tissue around the neck, between the scapulae and around the kidneys burns fat to generate heat, a process that consumes oxygen and glucose. A cold baby therefore becomes a hypoglycaemic and acidotic baby, which is why a temperature below 36.5 degrees Celsius is treated as significant rather than trivial. Warm the baby with skin-to-skin contact under a blanket, a hat, and a warm room, and recheck; persistent hypothermia in a newborn can be a sign of sepsis and not simply of a cool house.

In the other direction, a rectal temperature of 38.0 degrees Celsius, 100.4 Fahrenheit, or higher in a baby under twenty-eight days old is a medical emergency requiring immediate assessment, without exception and regardless of how well the baby appears. This is not excessive caution. Newborn immune function is immature, the classic localising signs of infection are absent, and serious bacterial infection with group B streptococcus, Escherichia coli, Listeria monocytogenes or herpes simplex virus can progress from a well-looking baby to septic shock in hours. Standard practice is a full septic screen including blood culture, urine culture and usually lumbar puncture, with empirical intravenous antibiotics started before results return. Between one and three months the approach is more graded but still urgent. Do not give paracetamol or ibuprofen to a febrile newborn to see whether it settles; masking fever delays the diagnosis that matters.

Beyond fever, a compact list of signs should prompt immediate medical contact at any hour. Breathing difficulty shows as a sustained respiratory rate above sixty, grunting on expiration, flaring of the nostrils, or drawing-in of the skin between and below the ribs and above the sternum. Any pause in breathing longer than twenty seconds, or any pause accompanied by colour change or floppiness, is apnoea. Blue or dusky discolouration of the lips, tongue or centre of the face indicates inadequate oxygenation. Green or bright yellow bilious vomiting suggests intestinal obstruction such as malrotation with volvulus, a surgical emergency in which delay costs bowel. Forceful projectile vomiting after feeds from around three weeks suggests pyloric stenosis. Blood in the stool or vomit, a tense bulging fontanelle, a stiff or arched neck, a rash of small purple spots that does not blanch under pressure, a seizure, or a baby who is difficult to rouse, floppy, or has stopped feeding all belong on the same list.

The general principle that matters more than any individual sign is change in behaviour. Newborns have a narrow behavioural repertoire, and a baby who is behaving differently from their own established baseline, particularly one who has become quiet and disinterested in feeding when they were previously vigorous, is communicating something. Parental instinct that something is wrong is a documented and clinically respected predictor. Trust it, present the baby for assessment, and accept being told that all is well as a good outcome rather than an embarrassment.

sections.heading: Screening, Vitamin K, Vaccination and the Well-Baby Schedule
sections.body:
A short sequence of preventive interventions is offered in the first hours and days, and each exists because of a specific, well-documented harm. Vitamin K is given as a single intramuscular injection of one milligram, or 0.5 milligrams for babies under about 1.5 kilograms, within six hours of birth. Newborns are physiologically deficient: vitamin K crosses the placenta poorly, breast milk contains very little, and the gut flora that will eventually synthesise it are not yet established. Without prophylaxis, late vitamin K deficiency bleeding occurs in roughly one in fourteen thousand to one in twenty-five thousand infants between two and twelve weeks, and about half of those cases present as intracranial haemorrhage with a mortality around twenty percent and permanent neurological damage in many survivors. The oral regimen is an alternative but requires multiple correctly timed doses and is measurably less effective.

Erythromycin or tetracycline eye ointment is applied in many countries to prevent gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum, which can destroy the cornea within days. The hepatitis B vaccine birth dose is given within twenty-four hours; perinatal infection carries a ninety percent chance of chronic carriage, against under ten percent when acquired in adulthood, and chronic carriage is what leads to cirrhosis and liver cancer decades later. Babies born to hepatitis B positive mothers additionally receive immunoglobulin.

Newborn screening is performed by a heel-prick blood spot, usually between twenty-four and forty-eight hours in most programmes, sometimes up to day five. The panel varies by country but generally includes congenital hypothyroidism, phenylketonuria, cystic fibrosis, sickle cell disease, medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency and a set of other inherited metabolic disorders. Every condition on the list shares a property: it causes irreversible damage before it causes symptoms, and early treatment prevents that damage. Untreated congenital hypothyroidism, for instance, causes profound and permanent intellectual disability, while a daily levothyroxine tablet started in the first weeks results in normal development. Two further screens are routine: pulse oximetry to detect critical congenital heart disease by comparing oxygen saturation in the right hand and a foot, and a hearing screen using otoacoustic emissions or automated auditory brainstem response, since early identification of deafness transforms language outcomes.

The follow-up schedule then continues with a newborn physical examination within seventy-two hours covering heart sounds, femoral pulses, red reflex of the eyes, palate, hips using the Ortolani and Barlow manoeuvres, and testes; a repeat examination at six to eight weeks; and weight and feeding checks in the first week or two. Primary immunisations generally begin at six to eight weeks with combined vaccines against diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, polio, Haemophilus influenzae type b, hepatitis B, pneumococcus, meningococcus and rotavirus depending on national schedule. Pertussis deserves specific mention because it is most lethal precisely in the window before the baby can be vaccinated, which is why maternal vaccination in pregnancy and cocooning of close contacts are recommended: maternal antibody transferred across the placenta protects the newborn during that gap.

sections.heading: Handling, Carrying, Car Seats and Everyday Physical Safety
sections.body:
A newborn's head is about a quarter of its total body length and roughly a quarter of its weight, and the neck muscles cannot yet support it, so every lift and every position change must include deliberate head support until around three to four months when head control emerges. To pick a baby up from a flat surface, slide one hand under the head and neck and the other under the bottom, then lift as a single unit rather than pulling on the arms. Supporting the head is not fragile handling for its own sake: uncontrolled flopping of the head strains the cervical spine, and violent shaking causes the shearing injuries of abusive head trauma. Ordinary walking, rocking and playful movement is entirely safe.

Car seats save lives and are also the single most commonly misused piece of infant equipment, with observational studies repeatedly finding error rates between fifty and ninety percent. A newborn must travel rear-facing, and should remain rear-facing as long as the seat permits, because in a frontal collision a rear-facing shell distributes force across the whole back of the head, neck and torso rather than loading it into a neck whose vertebrae are still partly cartilaginous. Never place a rear-facing seat in front of an active passenger airbag. The harness straps should emerge from slots at or just below the shoulders, and be tight enough that you cannot pinch a horizontal fold of webbing at the collarbone. The chest clip sits at armpit level, not on the abdomen. Bulky coats must come off before buckling, because they compress in a crash and leave several centimetres of slack; put a blanket over the fastened harness instead. The seat should recline at roughly forty-five degrees so the head does not fall forward and close off the airway.

That last point generalises beyond the car. Positional asphyxia is the reason a newborn should not be left sleeping in a car seat, bouncer, swing, sling worn incorrectly, or propped at an angle. In a carrier or sling, keep the baby close enough to kiss, with the face visible and uncovered, the chin off the chest with at least a finger's width of clearance, the back supported in a natural curve, and the hips in a spread-squat position. A newborn whose chin is pressed into the chest can suffocate silently.

Around the home, set the water heater to 49 degrees Celsius, install and test smoke alarms, never carry a hot drink while holding the baby, and keep cords, blind pulls, plastic bags and loose bedding out of the sleep space. Pets should never be left unsupervised with a newborn regardless of temperament. Anyone with a cold sore should not kiss a newborn: neonatal herpes simplex acquired in the first weeks carries substantial mortality and neurological damage, and the same reasoning underlies asking visitors with any respiratory infection to stay away and asking everyone to wash their hands. Second-hand smoke on clothing and in the home raises the risk of sudden infant death and respiratory illness, so smoking should happen outdoors, with a change of outer layer afterwards.

sections.heading: Bonding, Tummy Time and What Development Looks Like
sections.body:
Attachment is built through thousands of small, unremarkable interactions rather than a single bonding moment, and parents who feel no immediate rush of love at delivery are in ordinary company; surveys consistently find that a large minority of mothers describe affection developing over days or weeks. What drives attachment is contingent responsiveness: the baby signals, an adult responds within a few seconds in a way that matches the signal, and the baby learns that the world is predictable and that their own actions have effects. This is the foundation of both emotional security and early learning, and it is why responding promptly to a newborn's cries cannot spoil them. The capacity for deliberate manipulation requires cognitive machinery that does not exist for many months.

Skin-to-skin contact, sometimes called kangaroo care, is the most evidence-supported single practice in this area. Placing a naked baby, wearing only a nappy, upright on a parent's bare chest under a blanket stabilises heart rate, breathing and blood glucose, improves temperature regulation, reduces crying, promotes breastfeeding success, and in preterm infants reduces mortality substantially. It works for fathers and non-birth parents as well as mothers, and it remains useful well beyond the first days.

Sensory capacities in the newborn are specific. Vision is blurry, with acuity around 20/400, and focuses best at twenty to thirty centimetres, roughly the distance from the breast to a parent's face. High-contrast patterns and human faces attract the most attention. Hearing is well developed before birth, and newborns show preference for their mother's voice and for the language they heard in utero. Smell is acute enough that babies orient toward a pad worn against their own mother's breast. The most useful implication is that no toys or equipment are required: talking, singing, holding and letting the baby look at your face supplies exactly the input the developing brain is built to consume.

Tummy time is supervised prone play while awake, and it exists to counteract a real side effect of back-sleeping. Since back-to-sleep campaigns began, positional plagiocephaly, a flattening of one part of the skull, has become common, and prone play strengthens neck, shoulder and trunk muscles that support later rolling, sitting and crawling. Start from the first week with two or three sessions of a minute or two each, on a firm surface or lying on a parent's chest, building toward a cumulative fifteen to thirty minutes daily by around seven weeks and about an hour by three months. Many babies protest initially; short frequent sessions work better than long ones. Alternating the direction the head faces in the cot and limiting time in seats and swings also reduces flattening. Expect early milestones roughly as follows: brief head lifting in prone within the first weeks, a genuine responsive social smile at around six to eight weeks, cooing sounds by two months, and hands opening and coming to the midline by three months. Milestone ranges are wide, and preterm babies should be assessed on corrected age, subtracting the weeks of prematurity, until about two years.

sections.heading: Parental Recovery, Sleep Deprivation and Mental Health
sections.body:
The health of the adults is part of newborn care, not a separate topic, because an exhausted or unwell parent is a less safe carer. Physical recovery from birth takes longer than most people expect. Lochia, the postpartum vaginal discharge, continues for two to six weeks, moving from red through brown to yellowish-white. Perineal tears and episiotomy repairs are typically comfortable enough for normal walking by two weeks and healed by six. A caesarean is major abdominal surgery, and the standard advice to avoid lifting anything heavier than the baby for six weeks is about wound and fascial healing rather than delicacy. Afterpains, cramping as the uterus involutes, are strongest during breastfeeding because oxytocin acts on the uterus as well as the breast.

Several postpartum complications are genuine emergencies for the mother and are frequently missed because attention has shifted entirely to the baby. Bleeding that soaks a maternity pad in an hour, passes clots larger than a golf ball, or restarts heavily after slowing may indicate secondary postpartum haemorrhage. A severe headache, visual disturbance such as flashing lights, upper abdominal pain under the ribs, or sudden swelling of the face and hands can indicate postpartum pre-eclampsia, which can develop up to six weeks after delivery and can cause seizures. Fever above 38 degrees, foul-smelling discharge or abdominal tenderness suggests endometritis. Pain, swelling, redness or warmth in one calf, or breathlessness and chest pain, raise the possibility of venous thromboembolism, for which the risk is elevated for at least six weeks postpartum. A red, wedge-shaped, painful area of breast with flu-like symptoms is mastitis, which needs continued milk removal and often antibiotics, not weaning.

Mental health follows a distinct pattern. Baby blues affect somewhere between half and eighty percent of mothers, peak around days three to five as hormones fall, present as tearfulness, irritability and emotional lability, and resolve without treatment by about two weeks. Postnatal depression affects roughly ten to fifteen percent, may begin any time in the first year, and is distinguished by duration beyond two weeks and by functional impairment: persistent low mood or anhedonia, hopelessness, guilt, inability to sleep even when the baby sleeps, and intrusive thoughts. Around one in ten fathers and non-birth parents experience it too. Screening tools such as the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale are widely used, with a score of thirteen or more prompting further assessment, and any positive response to the item about self-harm requiring immediate attention.

Postpartum psychosis is rare, at one to two per thousand births, but it is a psychiatric emergency. It usually begins abruptly within the first two weeks with confusion, agitation, not sleeping at all, grandiose or paranoid beliefs, or hallucinations, and it carries real risk to both mother and baby. It requires urgent assessment the same day, not an appointment next week. On sleep, the practical arithmetic is that total nightly sleep matters less than obtaining at least one unbroken stretch of four to five hours; splitting the night into shifts, with one adult fully off duty and out of earshot, is usually more restorative than both adults waking for every feed.

sections.heading: Common Problems, Limits of Home Judgement, and What To Do When It Goes Wrong
sections.body:
Most of what goes wrong in the newborn period falls into a small number of recognisable patterns. Feeding difficulty is the most common and the most consequential, because it drives weight loss, dehydration and jaundice simultaneously. The usual causes are a shallow latch, a sleepy baby who does not feed long enough, delayed lactogenesis, or occasionally tongue-tie in which a tight lingual frenulum restricts tongue elevation. Tongue-tie is genuinely over-diagnosed and genuinely under-diagnosed depending on where you are; division is a minor procedure that helps when there is a real functional restriction with feeding impact, and helps nothing when performed on an asymptomatic anatomical variant. The right response to any feeding worry is early, skilled, in-person assessment from a lactation consultant, midwife or paediatric clinician, watching an actual feed. Advice given over the phone or from the internet cannot see a latch.

Reflux is the second great source of anxiety.
